works.medium: Sound film, black-and-white and colour, 35mm, two completed parts
works.description: A stylised, operatic two-part biography of the 16th-century tsar, shot with sharply angled lighting and stark, mask-like performances closer to Kabuki theatre than naturalistic acting. Part I won Eisenstein a Stalin Prize, but Stalin personally banned Part II for what he read as a veiled critique of his own purges; it was not released until 1958, a decade after Eisenstein's death, and a planned Part III was never completed.

credit.file: File:Ivan Grozny Cherkasov and Zharov by Moskvin.jpg
credit.author: Главархив Москвы

works.title: Self-Portrait (Self-Portrait 7)
works.location: National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi
works.description: Painted in Paris when she was 17, one of some 19 self-portraits she made in Europe. She leans toward the viewer, hair loose and shoulders bare, confident and playful. The painting shows how quickly she absorbed the lessons of Post-Impressionism and the European tradition of self-portraiture.

works.title: Three Girls (Group of Young Girls)
works.location: National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi
works.description: Three young Indian women sit close together, silent and withdrawn, their faces sombre and their clothes glowing in deep reds, greens and ochres. Painted soon after her return to India, it expresses the waiting and melancholy she saw in the lives of Indian women. It won the gold medal of the Bombay Art Society in 1937.

credit.file: File:Amrita Sher-Gil Group of Three Girls.jpg
credit.author: Amrita Sher-Gil

works.title: Bride's Toilet
works.location: National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi
works.description: Women prepare a young bride for her wedding: one combs her hair, another brings a tray, a child sits nearby. The bride's expression is quiet and uncertain. Part of her "South Indian trilogy", painted after her visit to the Ajanta caves, it combines the flat colour and flowing lines of ancient Indian murals with a modern, psychological intensity.

works.title: Brahmacharis
works.location: National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi
works.description: A group of young Brahmin students, bare-chested with sacred threads, sit on the ground in solemn contemplation. The dark skin tones set against white cloth and the monumental, simplified figures show the influence of the Ajanta frescoes. It is another painting from the South Indian trilogy.

works.title: Village Scene
works.description: Women sit talking beside a long, whitewashed house with red-barred windows, while a lone figure wrapped in a yellow shawl stands in the dusky courtyard near a ladder. The flat, glowing earth colours and still, simplified figures recall the Indian miniature painting that Sher-Gil studied closely after 1937. When it came up for auction in 2006, it sold for $1.6 million, then one of the highest prices ever paid for an Indian painting.

works.title: Haldi Grinders
works.location: National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi
works.description: Women in red and orange grind turmeric (*haldi*) under the shade of trees in a village courtyard. Painted at Saraya in Uttar Pradesh, where she lived in her last years, it has the decorative patterning and bright, flat colour of Indian miniatures, applied to the everyday labour of rural women.

artists.name: Enheduanna
artists.lifespan: flourishing around 2300 BCE; the span of about 2285–2250 BCE is only an estimate

works.title: Enheduanna
works.medium: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad
works.description:
Enheduanna (flourishing around 2300 BCE; the span of about 2285 to 2250 BCE is only an estimate) was a high priestess of the moon god Nanna at the Sumerian city of Ur and a daughter of Sargon of Akkad. She is often called the earliest author known by name, though her dates and the attribution of her texts are debated.

Enheduanna served as en-priestess of Nanna at Ur, appointed by her father Sargon of Akkad. Her dates depend on the chronology used.

A disc found at Ur in 1927 by Leonard Woolley's team shows a figure identified by inscription as Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon, in a ritual scene.

Sumerian poems are attributed to her, including 42 temple hymns and hymns to the goddess Inanna such as "The Exaltation of Inanna."

The surviving copies come from schools of the Old Babylonian period, about 1800 BCE, some five to six centuries after her lifetime, and scholars disagree about whether she wrote every attributed text.

In "The Exaltation of Inanna" the speaker describes being driven from office by a usurper, Lugal-ane, and restored; the historicity of this is debated.

credit.work: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad
credit.author: Mefman00

works.title: Nefertiti
works.description:
Nefertiti (about 1370 to about 1330 BCE) was the Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian king Akhenaten and is shown with unusual prominence in the art of his reign. Her exact birth and death dates and her burial place are uncertain, and the dates given are approximate.

Nefertiti married Akhenaten (then Amenhotep IV) early in his reign; the exact dates of the marriage are uncertain.

The couple promoted the worship of the sun disk Aten and moved the royal capital to a new city, Akhetaten (modern Amarna).

Reliefs and statues show Nefertiti at a scale and in roles usually reserved for the king, including taking part in rites for the Aten.

They had six daughters, including Meritaten and Ankhesenamun, who later married Tutankhamun.

Scholarship before 2012 assumed she vanished from the record around year 12 of the reign, but an inscription dated to year 16 names Neferneferuaten-Nefertiti alongside Akhenaten. Whether she died, changed title, or ruled as co-regent under the name Neferneferuaten is debated.

works.title: Akhenaten
works.description:
Akhenaten was an Egyptian pharaoh (reigned about 1353 to 1336 BCE) who promoted the worship of the sun disk Aten above the traditional gods.

He built a new capital at Akhetaten (modern Amarna).

Art of his reign has a distinctive, naturalistic style.

Traditional religion was restored soon after his death, under his successors including Tutankhamun.

His wife was Nefertiti.

works.title: Ramesses II
works.description:
Ramesses II (about 1303 to 1213 BCE), also called Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty. He ruled for about 66 years, fought the Hittites at Kadesh, made one of the earliest surviving peace treaties, and built temples across Egypt and Nubia.

Ramesses II came to the throne in 1279 BCE by the most widely used chronology and reigned until 1213 BCE. Other chronologies differ by several years.

About 1274 BCE he fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh, in present-day Syria. Both sides claimed victory. Ramesses had it carved on temple walls, though most historians think the Hittites gained more.

About 1259 BCE he made a treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III. It survives in Egyptian and Hittite versions, each saying the other side asked for peace first.

He built the capital Pi-Ramesses, the Ramesseum and the temples at Abu Simbel, moved in the 1960s to escape the Aswan High Dam reservoir. Many monuments carry his name over those of earlier kings.

He is estimated to have had more than 90 children and to have lived to about 90. His thirteenth son, Merneptah, succeeded him.

works.title: Fu Hao
works.medium: Fu Hao Tomb and Statue, c. 1200 BC, Reign of King Wu Ding, Shang Dynasty (101…
works.description:
Fu Hao (died about 1200 BCE) was a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding, named in oracle bone inscriptions as a military commander and a ritual leader. Her intact tomb, found in 1976, is among the richest of the Shang period. Her birth year is unknown.

Fu Hao is named in oracle bone inscriptions as a wife of the Shang king Wu Ding, whose reign is dated about 1250 to 1192 BCE, though dates vary by chronology. She is thought to have died about 1200 BCE.

The inscriptions record her leading military campaigns against neighboring groups and directing ritual sacrifices.

Her tomb (M5) at Yinxu, the Shang capital site near Anyang in Henan, was found undisturbed in 1976 by a team led by Zheng Zhenxiang.

It held 468 bronze objects and 755 jade objects, as well as hundreds of bone objects and thousands of cowry shells.

Inscriptions on many bronzes name her, Fu Hao, or "Mother Xin," which is the basis for identifying the tomb with the woman of the oracle bones.

credit.work: Fu Hao Tomb and Statue, c. 1200 BC, Reign of King Wu Ding, Shang Dynasty (10197821303)
credit.author: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China

works.title: Gilgamesh
works.description:
Gilgamesh was a king of the Sumerian city of Uruk, probably a real ruler of the Early Dynastic period sometime between about 2800 and 2500 BCE, who became the subject of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the earliest surviving major work of narrative literature.

The Sumerian King List names him as the fifth king of Uruk's first dynasty and credits him with an implausible 126-year reign, typical of the list's treatment of early rulers.

Later inscriptions, notably the Tummal Inscription written under Ishbi-Erra long after the Early Dynastic period, credit a king of this name with building the great city walls of Uruk, a claim the Epic itself repeats as Gilgamesh's lasting achievement.

The Epic, assembled from older Sumerian poems into its best-known Akkadian version around the 12th century BCE, follows Gilgamesh's friendship with the wild man Enkidu, his quest for immortality after Enkidu's death, and his eventual acceptance of mortality.

No securely contemporary royal inscription from Gilgamesh's own lifetime has been found, though one inscription possibly from a contemporary official at Ur may name him; most of what historians infer about a real Gilgamesh comes from later king lists, dedicatory inscriptions naming him, and the literary tradition itself.

credit.author: editor Austen Henry Layard , drawing by L. Gruner

works.title: Hammurabi
works.medium: F0182 Louvre Code Hammourabi Bas-relief Sb8 rwk
works.description:
Hammurabi was the king of Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE, who united much of Mesopotamia and is known for a famous inscribed law code.

The Code of Hammurabi, carved on a stone stele about 1754 BCE, lists 282 laws.

It sets penalties that vary by social class and includes the principle of proportionate punishment.

The stele was displayed publicly, making the law visible.

The original is in the Louvre in Paris.

credit.work: F0182 Louvre Code Hammourabi Bas-relief Sb8 rwk
credit.author: Mbzt

works.title: Hatshepsut
works.medium: Seated Statue of Hatshepsut MET Hatshepsut2012 (cropped)
works.description:
Hatshepsut was an Egyptian ruler of the 18th Dynasty who held the title of pharaoh, sharing the throne with Thutmose III, until her death in 1458 BCE. Her reign is traditionally dated 1479 to 1458 BCE, and she is one of the first women known to have held the office.

She first acted as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, then took the title of pharaoh around the seventh year of his reign (about 1473 BCE), sharing his regnal count.

She sponsored a trading expedition to Punt, on the Red Sea coast of Africa.

Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari is a major monument.

Many of her images were later removed or defaced, possibly after her death.

credit.work: Seated Statue of Hatshepsut MET Hatshepsut2012 (cropped)

works.title: Piye
works.description:
Piye (reigned about 744 to 714 BCE) was a king of Kush who conquered Egypt and is usually counted as the first ruler of Egypt's Twenty-fifth (Kushite) Dynasty. His birth year is unknown; the dates given here are those of his reign.

Piye ruled Kush from Napata, near Jebel Barkal in present-day Sudan. His reign is dated about 744 to 714 BCE; some scholars count his father Kashta as the dynasty's first ruler.

About 728 BCE he marched north against Tefnakht, prince of Sais, and a coalition of Delta rulers, and defeated them.

His Victory Stele, found at Jebel Barkal in 1862 and now in Cairo, records the campaign in Egyptian hieroglyphs, presents him as serving the god Amun, and lists the rulers who submitted to him.

He did not remain in Egypt; he returned to Kush and left local rulers in place.

He expanded the temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal.

works.title: Ashurbanipal
works.description:
Ashurbanipal (about 685 to about 631 BCE) was king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 669 BCE. He is known for his conquests, for the royal library at Nineveh, and for palace reliefs showing war and lion hunts.

Ashurbanipal was born about 685 BCE, a son of Esarhaddon, and became king of Assyria in 669 BCE, with his brother Shamash-shum-ukin as king of Babylon.

Assyrian forces sacked Thebes in Egypt in 663 BCE, ending Kushite rule in Egypt.

Shamash-shum-ukin rebelled in 652 BCE, and Ashurbanipal took Babylon in 648 BCE after a long war. In campaigns of about 647 to 646 BCE he defeated Elam, and Susa was destroyed in the campaign of about 646 BCE.

His libraries at Nineveh, found in the 19th century, held tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments, including a version of the Epic of Gilgamesh. He boasted of his own scribal education.

His inscriptions and reliefs record brutal treatment of defeated enemies, including mass deportation, mutilation and execution.

works.title: Sappho
works.description:
Sappho (about 630 to about 570 BCE) was a Greek lyric poet from the island of Lesbos whose songs of love, longing and ritual were collected in at least eight books, possibly nine, in antiquity. Only fragments survive, plus one complete poem.

Sappho was born about 630 BCE on Lesbos in the eastern Aegean, in Mytilene or Eresos according to ancient sources; her dates are approximate.

She composed songs in Aeolic Greek to be sung with a lyre, and the Sapphic stanza is named after her.

Ancient scholars gathered her poems in at least eight books, possibly nine. Only fragments survive, apart from one complete poem, a prayer to Aphrodite (Fragment 1).

New papyrus fragments published in 2004 and 2014 added lines, including a poem that mentions her brothers.

Many surviving poems express desire for women. Scholars debate whether her circle on Lesbos was a religious association, a school for girls, or a social group.

works.title: Confucius
works.description:
Confucius (Kong Fuzi, 551 to 479 BCE) was a Chinese teacher and thinker whose ideas about ethics, family, and government shaped East Asian societies for over two thousand years.

His sayings were collected by disciples in the Analects.

Central ideas include ren (humaneness), li (ritual propriety), and filial piety.

He was not widely influential during his lifetime; his ideas rose to prominence under the Han dynasty.

Confucian learning later became the basis of the imperial civil service examinations.

works.title: Darius I
works.description:
Darius I (about 550 to 486 BCE) was king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire from 522 BCE. He organized its provinces, began the building of Persepolis, and recorded his rise to power in the Behistun Inscription.

Darius I was born about 550 BCE and became king in 522 BCE after the death of Cambyses II. He put down revolts across the empire in his first years.

The Behistun Inscription, carved on a cliff in western Iran, tells the story of his rise in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Scholars debate whether its account of a usurper, Gaumata, is accurate, and Aramaic copies of the text have been found in Egypt.

He divided the empire into provinces (satrapies) under governors and issued a standard gold coin, the daric.

He is credited with the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa and began the terrace at Persepolis about 518 BCE, though sources differ and the earliest surviving remains there date to about 515 BCE.

His inscriptions honor the god Ahura Mazda.

The Behistun Inscription, carved on a cliff in western Iran, tells the story of his rise in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Scholars debate whether its account of a usurper, Gaumata, is accurate, and Aramaic copies of the text have been found in Egypt.

He divided the empire into provinces (satrapies) under governors and issued a standard gold coin, the daric.

He is credited with the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa and began the terrace at Persepolis about 518 BCE, though sources differ and the earliest surviving remains there date to about 515 BCE.

His inscriptions honor the god Ahura Mazda.

works.title: Sun Tzu
works.description:
Sun Tzu (traditionally about 544 to 496 BCE) is the name attached to The Art of War, the most influential text on military strategy from ancient China, said to have served the state of Wu. Whether he was one historical person is disputed.

Tradition places Sun Tzu, personal name Sun Wu, as a general who advised King Helü of Wu in the late 6th century BCE. The Art of War is organized in about 13 short chapters.

The historian Sima Qian, writing centuries later, told a story of Sun Tzu proving his discipline by drilling the king's concubines, executing two who disobeyed. Scholars treat this as legend.

His name appears in no text earlier than Sima Qian's history, and one theory holds "Sun Wu" was a made-up title, with the Art of War actually the work of his supposed descendant Sun Bin.

In 1972 bamboo strips from a Han tomb at Yinqueshan included versions of both the Art of War and a separate text by Sun Bin, confirming the Art of War circulated early and that Sun Bin was a distinct author.

The text has shaped military and business thought for over two thousand years, and is translated worldwide.

works.title: Cyrus the Great
works.description:
Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 6th century BCE by conquering the Medes, Lydia, and Babylon.

His birth date is uncertain, with scholars giving about 600 to 576 BCE.

He defeated the Median king Astyages around 550 BCE and the Lydian king Croesus around 547 BCE.

He took Babylon in 539 BCE.

The Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian clay cylinder found in 1879, records his account of the conquest and his restoration of gods and deported peoples.

He died in 530 BCE campaigning on the eastern frontier and was buried at Pasargadae.

works.title: Dido
works.description:
Dido, also called Elissa, is the legendary founder-queen of Carthage, traditionally said to have led Phoenician settlers from Tyre to found the city on the North African coast around 814 BCE; her birth and death dates are not historically fixed.

The earliest known account of her founding of Carthage comes from the Greek historian Timaeus of Tauromenium, writing in the 4th to 3rd century BCE, centuries after the traditional founding date.

Tradition holds she fled Tyre after her brother, King Pygmalion, murdered her husband to seize his wealth, and that she later took her own life rather than marry a local Libyan king, Iarbas, who threatened war.

No Phoenician inscription or contemporary record names a founder called Dido or Elissa; archaeological evidence of Phoenician settlement at the site of Carthage has so far been found only from the last quarter of the 8th century BCE, about a century or more after the traditional founding date, though it may still fit a folk memory of an organized colonizing expedition.

Her best-known appearance, as the doomed lover of the Trojan hero Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, is a literary invention: the Trojan War's traditional date is centuries before Carthage's traditional founding, so the two could not have met.

works.title: Laozi
works.description:
Laozi (Lao Tzu, "Old Master") is the traditional author of the Daodejing and a founding figure of Daoism, said to have lived in the 6th century BCE. Whether he was a single historical person is disputed.

Laozi is traditionally placed in the 6th century BCE, in the time of Confucius. The date is uncertain and no date of death is known.

The historian Sima Qian, writing about 100 BCE, identifies him as Li Er, keeper of archives at the Zhou court, and also lists other men who might have been meant, so the uncertainty was already old.

Sima Qian's account says he met Confucius, then left the Zhou domain to the west and wrote the text at the Hangu Pass at the request of the gatekeeper Yin Xi. This account is traditional.

The Daodejing has about 5,000 Chinese characters in 81 short chapters. Its earliest excavated versions, from Guodian (about 300 BCE) and Mawangdui (tomb sealed 168 BCE), fit the view of most scholars that the text took shape in the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE.

Later religious Daoism honored him as a deity, Laojun, and the Tang dynasty's imperial family, named Li, claimed him as an ancestor.

works.title: Siddhartha Gautama
works.description:
Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha, was a spiritual teacher in northern India whose teachings founded Buddhism. Traditional dates are about 563 to 483 BCE, but modern scholarship suggests a somewhat later range.

Buddhist tradition holds that he left a princely life and attained awakening at Bodh Gaya.

His teachings include the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.

The exact dates of his life are debated among scholars.

Buddhism later spread across Asia via monks and trade routes.

works.title: Tomyris
works.description:
Tomyris was a queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic people east of the Caspian Sea, who according to the Greek historian Herodotus defeated and killed Cyrus the Great of Persia in 530 BCE. She is known only from Herodotus, and other ancient accounts of Cyrus's death differ.

Tomyris appears only in Book 1 of Herodotus's Histories, written about a century after the events. Her dates are unknown; the date given here is that of the battle in his account.

Herodotus says she ruled the Massagetae, who lived east of the Caspian Sea near the Araxes River, and rejected Cyrus's offer of marriage, which he saw as a way to gain her kingdom.

In his account the Persians captured her son Spargapises by trickery, and he killed himself in captivity. Tomyris then defeated the Persian army in battle.

Herodotus says she had Cyrus's body found and his head put in a wineskin filled with blood.

Other ancient accounts differ: Xenophon has Cyrus die peacefully in his palace, and Ctesias has him die of a wound in a war on the eastern frontier that the Persians won.

artists.name: Gorgo
artists.lifespan: born about 518 BCE, last attested around 480 BCE

works.title: Gorgo
works.description:
Gorgo (born about 518 BCE, last attested around 480 BCE) was queen of Sparta as the wife of King Leonidas I, remembered by the historian Herodotus as unusually sharp-witted and politically perceptive for a woman in his account of Greek affairs.

She was the daughter of the Spartan king Cleomenes I and, according to Herodotus, advised him as a child not to trust a bribe offered by an Ionian envoy seeking Spartan military aid.

Herodotus credits her with detecting a warning about the Persian king Xerxes's invasion plans hidden on a wax-covered writing tablet sent by the exiled Spartan king Demaratus, when other Spartans could not work out its message.

She was the wife of Leonidas I, who died leading the defense of Thermopylae against the Persian invasion in 480 BCE, the same year in which she is last clearly attested in the sources.

Nearly everything known of her comes from Herodotus's Histories, written decades after her lifetime, and no independent Spartan record of her actions survives.

works.title: Pericles
works.description:
Pericles (about 495 to 429 BCE) was the leading Athenian statesman for over three decades in the mid-5th century BCE, a period later called the Golden Age of Athens for its building programs, drama, and democratic institutions.

He rose to prominence in Athenian democracy through the office of strategos (general), to which he was re-elected yearly, using his influence over the Assembly rather than any formal single office to shape policy.

He directed the building program on the Acropolis, including the Parthenon, funded partly by treasury funds originally collected from the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states organized against Persia.

He extended pay for jury service and other public roles to poorer citizens, broadening practical participation in Athenian democracy beyond the wealthy.

He championed the aggressive strategy that led Athens into the Peloponnesian War against Sparta in 431 BCE, and died of plague in 429 BCE during the war's early years, before its outcome was decided.

works.title: Aristotle
works.description:
Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and scientist who studied logic, ethics, politics, physics, and biology, and tutored Alexander of Macedon.

He studied under Plato in Athens and later founded his own school, the Lyceum.

He wrote on logic, ethics, politics, poetics, physics, and biology.

His biological work involved careful observation of marine life.

His works were preserved and extended in the Islamic world and later in Latin Europe.

works.title: Alexander the Great
works.medium: Alexander Mosaic detail of Alexander the Great (3x4 cropped)
works.description:
Alexander III of Macedon (356 to 323 BCE) was a military commander who conquered the Persian Empire and spread Greek influence from Egypt to India.

He became king at about twenty after the assassination of his father, Philip II.

He won major battles at Issus and Gaugamela against the Persian king Darius III.

His army turned back at the Hyphasis (Beas) river in India.

He died in Babylon in 323 BCE; his empire was divided among his generals.

works.title: Chandragupta Maurya
works.description:
Chandragupta Maurya (about 340 to 297 BCE) founded the Maurya Empire, the first political power to unite most of the Indian subcontinent, after overthrowing the Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 321 BCE.

With guidance from the strategist Chanakya (Kautilya), Chandragupta seized the throne of Magadha and took the throne of Magadha. The Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft traditionally attributed to Chanakya, was long linked to his administration, but most scholars now date it to roughly the 1st to 3rd centuries CE and doubt that it describes his reign.

Between about 305 and 303 BCE he fought the Diadoch ruler Seleucus I Nicator; the resulting settlement ceded territory in the northwest to the Maurya and included a marriage alliance, while Seleucus received war elephants in return.

The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, sent to Chandragupta's court at Pataliputra, wrote the Indica, a major but now fragmentary source on Mauryan India.

Later Jain tradition holds that Chandragupta abdicated, became an ascetic under Bhadrabahu, and died by ritual fasting (sallekhana) at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, though this account survives mainly in sources written well after his reign.

works.title: Ashoka
works.medium: Ashoka's visit to the Ramagrama stupa Sanchi Stupa 1 Southern gateway
works.description:
Ashoka (about 304 to 232 BCE) was a Mauryan emperor who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent and became a patron of Buddhism after a bloody war.

He conquered the region of Kalinga around 261 BCE at great human cost; his own edicts record about 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported.

He had edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars across his empire, promoting 'dhamma' (moral conduct).

He supported the spread of Buddhism, including missions abroad.

His lion capital is now a national emblem of India.

works.title: Qin Shi Huang
works.description:
Qin Shi Huang (259 to 210 BCE) was the first emperor of a unified China, who standardized writing, currency, and measures and built a large tomb complex including the terracotta army.

He became king of Qin at thirteen and completed the unification of China in 221 BCE.

He standardized the script, weights and measures, and axle widths.

Later historians, hostile to the Qin, described book burning and harsh punishments; some of these accounts are debated.

His tomb complex near Xi'an contains thousands of life-size clay soldiers.

works.title: Augustus
works.description:
Augustus (63 BCE to 14 CE) was the first Roman emperor, who ended a century of civil war and built the imperial system that lasted for centuries.

Born Gaius Octavius, he was the adopted heir of Julius Caesar.

After defeating rivals, he took the name Augustus in 27 BCE while keeping republican forms.

His reign began the Pax Romana, a long period of relative stability.

He reorganized the army, provinces, and taxation.

works.title: Ambiorix
works.description:
Ambiorix (active 54 to 53 BCE) was co-ruler of the Eburones, a Belgic tribe in what is now eastern Belgium, remembered for destroying a Roman legion during a revolt against Julius Caesar's occupation of Gaul.

He shared kingship of the Eburones with an older co-ruler, Cativolcus, an arrangement Caesar's own account describes but does not fully explain.

In the winter of 54 BCE he lured a Roman force under Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta out of its fortified camp with false promises of safe passage, then ambushed and destroyed it, killing both commanders.

Caesar responded with a campaign of deliberate devastation against the Eburones intended to eliminate the tribe entirely, but Ambiorix himself escaped capture and vanishes from the historical record after 53 BCE.

Nearly everything known about him comes from Caesar's own Commentarii de Bello Gallico, written to justify Caesar's conduct of the war to a Roman audience.

works.title: Ban Zhao
works.description:
Ban Zhao (about 45 to about 117 CE) was a Chinese historian and scholar of the Eastern Han dynasty who helped complete the Book of Han after her brother's death and wrote Lessons for Women. She was also a tutor and adviser at court.

Ban Zhao was born about 45 CE (some sources say about 49) into a scholarly family. Her father Ban Biao and her brother Ban Gu wrote much of the Book of Han (Hanshu), a history of the Western Han dynasty.

Ban Gu died in prison in 92 CE with the history unfinished, and Ban Zhao helped complete it by supplying the missing part of the Eight Tables.

She served at the imperial court as a tutor to the empress and her ladies and, from about 106 CE, as an adviser to the regent Empress Deng.

She is believed to have written Lessons for Women (Nüjie), in seven chapters, about 106 CE, though the date is not firmly established. It argues that girls should be educated and sets out rules of conduct for wives.

Later writers used Lessons for Women as a standard text for teaching girls obedience, and modern scholars disagree on whether it reinforced or challenged limits on women.

works.title: Trajan
works.description:
Trajan (53 to 117 CE) was Roman emperor from 98 to 117, presiding over the empire's greatest territorial extent and a major program of public building and infrastructure across the Roman world.

Born in Hispania, in present-day Spain, he was the first Roman emperor born outside Italy, adopted as heir by the emperor Nerva in 97 after a career as a successful general.

His conquest of Dacia, commemorated in the reliefs of Trajan's Column in Rome, added a wealthy new province rich in gold mines north of the Danube.

He extended Roman territory to its largest extent by annexing Armenia and parts of Mesopotamia after a campaign against the Parthian Empire late in his reign, gains his successor Hadrian largely abandoned as unsustainable.

His building programs included Trajan's Forum and Market in Rome, a new harbor at Ostia, and an extensive network of roads and bridges across the provinces, funded substantially by Dacian gold.

works.title: Zenobia
works.description:
Zenobia (Septimia Zenobia; about 240 to after 272) was queen of the caravan city of Palmyra in present-day Syria. She ruled for her young son and briefly extended Palmyrene control over Roman Egypt, Syria and much of Anatolia before the emperor Aurelian defeated her in 272.

Zenobia was the wife of Odaenathus, the ruler of Palmyra who had fought the Sasanian Persians for Rome in the 260s. He was killed about 267, and she took power as regent for their son Vaballathus.

About 270 her forces took Roman Egypt and pushed into Anatolia. By 271 she and her son used the titles Augusta and Augustus.

Some coins struck in 271 and 272 show Aurelian on one side and Vaballathus on the other, so her claim was for a time framed inside the Roman order.

Aurelian defeated her armies in 272 at Immae and Emesa and captured her. Palmyra was sacked in 273 after a revolt.

Her fate is unknown. One tradition says she was shown in Aurelian's triumph in 274; its source, the Historia Augusta, is often unreliable.

works.title: Ba Trieu
works.description:
Ba Trieu (Trieu Thi Trinh; birth year unknown, died 248 CE) led an uprising against the Chinese Eastern Wu administration of northern Vietnam in 248 CE, becoming a lasting symbol of Vietnamese resistance to foreign rule.

She is said to have raised a rebel force in Cuu Chan, in present-day Thanh Hoa province, at about age twenty, alongside her brother Trieu Quoc Dat.

Later chronicles describe her riding into battle on an elephant in gold-decorated armor, though these vivid details come from accounts written many centuries after her death rather than contemporary record.

Eastern Wu sent the general Lu Yin to suppress the revolt; after several months of fighting, her forces were defeated later in 248.

Vietnamese tradition holds that she fled to Bo Dien commune and died by suicide rather than be captured, with her burial place attributed to Mount Tung in Hau Loc District, while Chinese-source summaries have Lu Yin putting her to death (sources give no age at death); a temple to her still stands near the site.

works.title: Hypatia
works.medium: AI illustration: An empty lecture hall in a grand library
works.description:
Hypatia (about 350 to 415 CE) was a philosopher, mathematician, and astronomer in Alexandria, who taught many students and was murdered by a mob.

She was the daughter of the mathematician Theon and taught Neoplatonist philosophy.

She is credited with commentaries on mathematical works; the details are uncertain.

In 415 she was killed by a Christian mob during a political dispute between the Roman governor Orestes and Bishop Cyril.

Later writers turned her into a symbol, so historical and legendary accounts are mixed.

works.title: Attila
works.medium: Attila et les Huns par Georges-Antoine Rochegrosse
works.description:
Attila (about 406 to 453) was ruler of the Huns from 434, first with his brother Bleda and from about 445 alone. He led Hunnic armies against the Eastern and Western Roman empires, and almost all written sources about him were composed by Greeks and Romans.

Attila's birth year is uncertain, with estimates from the 390s to the early 400s. He became joint ruler in 434 and sole ruler after Bleda died, probably about 445.

After the Treaty of Margus (435) the Eastern Roman Empire doubled its yearly gold tribute, and after 443 it is reported to have reached 2,100 Roman pounds.

In 451 he invaded Gaul and fought a Roman and Visigothic army at the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 he invaded northern Italy. He withdrew both times.

He died in 453 after his wedding to Ildico. Priscus, as reported by Jordanes, describes a severe bleed. A later claim that his wife killed him is rejected by most historians. His empire broke up within a few years.

Priscus, an envoy who visited his court in 449, left the only known eyewitness description. Attila's capital and tomb have not been found.

works.title: Amanirenas
works.medium: Bronze head from an over-life-sized statue of Augustus, found in the ancient …
works.description:
Amanirenas was a queen (kandake) of the Kingdom of Kush who led the war against Roman Egypt from about 25 to 22 BCE and won a peace settlement from Augustus. Her birth and death years are unknown; the dates given here mark her approximate reign, about 40 to 10 BCE.

Amanirenas ruled Kush from its capital region around Meroë; her birth and death years are unknown, and her reign is estimated.

About 25 BCE Kushite forces attacked the Roman frontier in southern Egypt, taking towns including Syene, Elephantine and Philae, while the Roman prefect's army was away.

The prefect Gaius Petronius counterattacked about 24 BCE and sacked the Kushite city of Napata.

Peace was negotiated with Augustus about 21 to 20 BCE on Samos; Kush is reported to have paid no tribute.

The Greek geographer Strabo describes a one-eyed, mannish queen "Candace" who led the Kushites; scholars generally identify her as Amanirenas.

works.title: Amanitore
works.medium: Aegyptisches Museum Berlin InvNr7261 20080313 Barkenuntersatz Natakamani Aman…
works.description:
Amanitore was a queen of the kingdom of Kush who co-ruled from the capital Meroe alongside a king, Natakamani, usually thought to be her son, during a prosperous period in the middle of the 1st century CE.

Kushite royal women held the title kandake, often rendered "candace"; inscriptions and temple reliefs show Amanitore depicted with the same royal regalia and war imagery as Natakamani, suggesting genuinely shared rule rather than a purely ceremonial role.

The pair sponsored a major building program, including temples at Meroe, Naqa and Amara, among the best-preserved Kushite monuments to survive.

A relief at the Lion Temple at Naqa shows Amanitore, like Natakamani, smiting bound captives, an image of royal power normally reserved for kings elsewhere in the Nile Valley tradition.

Her exact reign dates are not fixed by any king list; estimates for the coregency center on the middle of the 1st century CE, though some run earlier, and it is sometimes placed as contemporary with the Roman emperor Nero.

credit.author: Sven-Steffen Arndt

works.title: Cleopatra VII
works.description:
Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, who allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony and died in 30 BCE after their defeat by Octavian.

She belonged to the Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great.

Ancient sources say she spoke several languages and, unlike most of her Ptolemaic predecessors, learned Egyptian.

She had a son with Julius Caesar and children with Mark Antony.

Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE.

After her death in 30 BCE, Egypt became a Roman province.

works.title: Ezana of Aksum
works.description:
Ezana was king of Aksum, in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, from about 320 to about 360 CE, though sources differ on the exact dates. He is known for adopting Christianity and for a campaign in the Nile valley, and his inscriptions and coins record both.

Ezana came to the throne as a child and ruled the Kingdom of Aksum from about 320 until about 360. Dates for his life and reign are approximate, and sources differ.

His early inscriptions and coins show older Aksumite religion, including a crescent and disc on his coins.

Frumentius, a Christian from Tyre (described as Phoenician, and in some accounts Syrian) who rose in the Aksumite court, is reported to have been consecrated Aksum's first bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, traditionally in 328, though other accounts say between 340 and 346.

Ezana converted to Christianity in the 4th century, though the exact date is uncertain. His later inscriptions invoke a "Lord of Heaven," and his coins replace the crescent and disc with the cross, which is often described as among the earliest coins to do so.

His inscriptions are in Ge'ez, Sabaean and Greek.

works.title: Trưng Sisters
works.description:
The Trưng Sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị (Chinese Zheng Ce and Zheng Er), led a revolt against Han Chinese rule in northern Vietnam from 40 to 43 CE. Their birth years are unknown; the dates given here are those of the revolt.

The Trưng Sisters came from Mê Linh in the Red River region, then part of the Han commandery of Jiaozhi.

They began the revolt in 40 CE. Chinese sources link it to harsh rule by the Han governor Su Ding, and Vietnamese tradition adds that he executed Trưng Trắc's husband, Thi Sách.

They took towns in several southern commanderies and are recorded as ruling as queens for about three years.

The Han general Ma Yuan led an army south and defeated them by 43 CE.

The Chinese history Hou Hanshu says they were captured and beheaded, while Vietnamese tradition says they drowned themselves in a river; this second account is traditional.

works.title: Khadija bint Khuwaylid
works.description:
Khadija bint Khuwaylid (about 555 to 619) was a merchant of Mecca and the first wife of Muhammad. Her dates and many details come from Muslim biographies written more than a century after her death.

Khadija belonged to the Quraysh tribe of Mecca and, according to tradition, financed trading caravans to Syria and hired agents to lead them.

Tradition says Muhammad led one of her caravans and that she proposed marriage, about 595. Accounts differ on her age then, and a common figure is 40.

Muslim tradition holds that she was the first person to accept Muhammad's message after his first revelation, about 610.

Tradition names four daughters, including Fatima, and sons who died young.

She died about 619, shortly before Muhammad's move to Medina in 622, a year remembered as the Year of Sorrow.

works.title: Muhammad
works.description:
Muhammad (about 570 to 632 CE) was an Arabian religious and political leader, regarded by Muslims as the last prophet, who founded the community that became the Islamic world.

He was born in Mecca and, according to Islamic tradition, began receiving revelations around 610, later compiled as the Quran.

In 622 he and his followers migrated to Medina (the Hijra), the start of the Islamic calendar.

By his death, most of the Arabian Peninsula had joined the community.

Islam is now followed by roughly a quarter of the world's population.

works.title: Xuanzang
works.description:
Xuanzang (602 to 664) was a Chinese Buddhist monk who traveled overland to India from 629 to 645 in search of authentic scriptures, studied for years at the monastery of Nalanda, and returned to translate texts and record his journey.

Xuanzang was born in 602 and ordained as a monk in his youth. In 629 he left China without imperial permission, traveling west through Central Asia toward India.

He spent years studying at Nalanda, a major center of Buddhist learning, under the scholar Silabhadra, and visited Buddhist sites across the subcontinent.

He returned to China in 645 with Buddhist texts, images and relics, and was welcomed by the Tang court despite his earlier unauthorized departure.

With official support he led a translation effort that produced more than a thousand fascicles of Buddhist texts rendered from Sanskrit into Chinese.

He also wrote the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, a travel account whose distances and descriptions later helped archaeologists locate sites such as Nalanda itself.

works.title: Pakal the Great
works.medium: Ajuar funerario de Pakal el Grande (Museo Nacional de Antropología)
works.description:
Pakal the Great (K'inich Janaab' Pakal, 603 to 683) ruled the Maya city of Palenque, in present-day Chiapas, Mexico, from 615 until his death, a reign of about 68 years.

Pakal was born in 603 and became king at age 12 in 615.

Palenque's inscriptions name his mother, Ix Sak K'uk', and show her presenting him with the crown at his accession.

During his reign the Palace complex at Palenque was enlarged and decorated with carved panels and hieroglyphic texts.

The Temple of the Inscriptions was built as his funerary monument and carries long hieroglyphic panels on Palenque's dynastic history.

In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier reached a burial chamber inside it, holding a carved stone sarcophagus and a jade mosaic mask.

works.title: Aisha bint Abi Bakr
works.medium: Battle of the Camel by Mirkhwand
works.description:
Aisha bint Abi Bakr (about 614 to 678 CE) was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad and a daughter of the first caliph, Abu Bakr. She is credited with transmitting more than two thousand hadith and took part in the Battle of the Camel in 656.

Aisha was born about 614 in Mecca to Abu Bakr and Umm Ruman. She died in Medina in July 678 (58 AH), a date that is uncertain.

Her marriage to Muhammad was contracted in Mecca and began in Medina about 623. Classical sources give her age as six or seven at the contract and nine at the start. These figures come from later hadith and biographies, and some modern scholars question them.

She is credited with more than 2,000 hadith on ritual, inheritance, ethics and daily life, found in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and she also taught.

In 656 she opposed Ali ibn Abi Talib, demanding punishment of the killers of the caliph Uthman. Her forces lost the Battle of the Camel near Basra. Ali pardoned her, and she withdrew from politics.

Sunni tradition honors her as a scholar. Shia tradition views her critically because of her opposition to Ali.

credit.work: Battle of the Camel by Mirkhwand
credit.author: Mirkhwand (d. 1498)

works.title: Wu Zetian
works.medium: 唐后行從圖 (局部) - 武則天
works.description:
Wu Zetian (624 to 705 CE) was the only woman to rule China in her own name as emperor, founding the short-lived Zhou dynasty (690 to 705).

She entered the palace as a concubine of the Tang emperor and later became empress consort.

She ruled effectively for decades before taking the throne herself in 690.

She expanded the civil service examination system to draw in talent from beyond the aristocracy.

She supported Buddhism.

works.title: Seondeok
works.description:
Queen Seondeok (birth year unknown, died 647 CE) ruled the Korean kingdom of Silla as its first reigning queen, a period marked by Buddhist temple building, early astronomical observation and continued warfare with the rival kingdoms of Baekje and Goguryeo.

She succeeded her father, King Jinpyeong, in 632 after he left no surviving son, becoming Silla's first female monarch in her own right.

Her reign saw the construction of Cheomseongdae, often described as one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia, and the Hwangnyongsa nine-story pagoda, built to help protect the kingdom according to Buddhist belief.

Silla faced repeated attacks from Baekje during her reign, including the loss of border fortresses, and she decided to form a military alliance with Tang China, with her general Kim Yushin and diplomat Kim Chunchu, later King Muyeol, traditionally credited with the negotiations.

A rebellion by the noble Bidam against her rule broke out in 647 and was suppressed by Kim Yushin and Kim Alcheon shortly after her death that same year, which some accounts link to the unrest.

works.title: Lady Six Sky
works.medium: MA D367 Maya stela 24, Naranjo, Guatemala
works.description:
Lady Six Sky (Wak Chanil Ajaw; active 682 to 741 CE) was a Maya noblewoman from Dos Pilas who arrived at Naranjo in 682 and effectively ruled the city for decades, restoring it after a period of defeat.

She was a daughter of the Dos Pilas king B'alaj Chan K'awiil, part of a network of the powerful city of Calakmul's allies against its rival Tikal.

Naranjo's royal line had been broken after a defeat by Caracol, and Lady Six Sky was installed there in 682, apparently to re-establish the dynasty.

Monuments record her overseeing military campaigns and presiding over her young son K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Chaahk's accession in 693, after which she continued to appear on inscriptions as a ruling figure into the 700s.

She never took the full royal title used by male kings of Naranjo, and continued to use the emblem glyph of her home city Dos Pilas throughout her life, so her exact formal status is debated by epigraphers.

credit.work: MA D367 Maya stela 24, Naranjo, Guatemala
credit.author: Unknown author Unknown author

works.title: Charlemagne
works.description:
Charlemagne (c. 748 to 814) was king of the Franks who conquered much of western and central Europe and was crowned emperor by the pope in Rome on Christmas Day 800.

He became sole king of the Franks in 771.

He conquered the Lombards in Italy, the Saxons, and parts of Spain's northern border.

Pope Leo III crowned him emperor on 25 December 800.

His court promoted a revival of learning, the Carolingian Renaissance, and the spread of a clear minuscule script.

His empire was divided among his descendants after his death in 814 and, under the Treaty of Verdun in 843, split into three kingdoms.

credit.author: Charlemagne. Autorité émettrice de monnaie indéterminé. Atelier monétaire. Émetteur

works.title: Al-Khwarizmi
works.medium: Madrid - Ciudad Universitaria, Monumento a Muhammad al-Juarismi (cropped)
works.description:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (about 780 to 850 CE) was a Persian scholar at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad whose work on algebra and Hindu-Arabic numerals shaped mathematics.

His book on 'al-jabr' (restoration) gave algebra its name.

The word 'algorithm' derives from the Latinized form of his name.

His work helped introduce Hindu-Arabic numerals and place-value arithmetic to the wider world.

He also compiled astronomical tables and geographical data.

credit.work: Madrid - Ciudad Universitaria, Monumento a Muhammad al-Juarismi (cropped)
credit.author: Zarateman

works.title: Basil II
works.description:
Basil II (958 to 1025) was Byzantine emperor for nearly fifty years, the longest reign in Roman or Byzantine imperial history, remembered above all for his decades-long war against the First Bulgarian Empire.

He became co-emperor as a child in 960 but did not gain full personal control of the government until about 989, when he was in his thirties, after suppressing rebellions by powerful aristocratic generals including Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas.

His long campaigns against Bulgaria culminated in the decisive Battle of Kleidion in 1014, after which Bulgaria was absorbed into the Byzantine Empire by 1018, earning him the later epithet "Bulgar-slayer" (Boulgaroktonos).

A story recorded by later chroniclers claims he blinded thousands of Bulgarian prisoners after Kleidion, leaving one eye to each of every hundredth man to lead the rest home; modern historians debate how literally this account should be taken.

He left the imperial treasury full and the empire at its greatest territorial extent since the 7th century, but died without an heir, and the strong central rule he had imposed did not survive his less capable successors.

works.title: Al-Biruni
works.description:
Al-Biruni (973 to after 1048) was a scholar from Khwarazm in Central Asia who wrote on astronomy, mathematics, geography, chronology and India. His Kitab al-Hind (about 1030) is a major medieval study of Indian science, religion and customs.

Al-Biruni was born in 973 in Kath, in Khwarazm in present-day Uzbekistan, and died after 1048, perhaps about 1050.

After the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud conquered Khwarazm in 1017, he was taken to Ghazni, where he worked under Mahmud and his successors.

He spent years in northwestern India, learned Sanskrit, and wrote the Kitab al-Hind, describing Indian science, religion, society and customs from Sanskrit texts and conversations with Indian scholars.

His Chronology of Ancient Nations (about 1000) compares the calendars and dating systems of many cultures.

He calculated the radius of the Earth as about 6,320 km by measuring the dip of the horizon from the top of a hill, close to the modern value.

works.title: Murasaki Shikibu
works.description:
Murasaki Shikibu (about 973 to about 1014) was a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court in the Heian period. She wrote The Tale of Genji, a 54-chapter novel of court life that is widely called the world's first novel.

"Murasaki Shikibu" is a later nickname. Her personal name is unknown; the nickname combines a character from her novel with her father's court rank.

She was born about 973 into a minor branch of the Fujiwara clan and learned the Chinese classics, normally reserved for men, by absorbing lessons given to her brother.

She married a much older provincial governor about 998 and was widowed within a few years. About 1005 or 1006 she entered court service as a lady-in-waiting to Empress Shōshi.

The Tale of Genji follows a fictional prince and, in its later chapters, his descendants. It may have been begun before she came to court, though sources suggest she likely composed it while serving as a lady-in-waiting, possibly chapter by chapter.

She wrote almost entirely in hiragana, the script associated with women's writing at court, and set many waka poems into the story as the characters' own compositions.

works.title: Ibn Sina
works.description:
Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980 to 1037) was a Persian physician and philosopher whose 'Canon of Medicine' became a standard medical text in the Islamic world and Europe for centuries.

He was born near Bukhara in Central Asia.

The Canon of Medicine (completed about 1025) organized medical knowledge in a systematic way.

It was translated into Latin and used in European universities into the 17th century.

His philosophical 'Book of Healing' also influenced medieval Europe.

works.title: Harald Hardrada
works.description:
Harald Hardrada (about 1015 to 1066) was King of Norway from 1046 to 1066, a warrior-king whose career took him from exile through mercenary service in Byzantium to the throne, and whose death at Stamford Bridge is often used to mark the end of the Viking Age.

After his half-brother King Olaf II was killed in battle in 1030, the teenage Harald fled Norway and eventually served as a commander in the Byzantine Empire's elite Varangian Guard, campaigning in the Mediterranean and Middle East.

He returned to Scandinavia around 1045 with substantial wealth, and secured a share of the Norwegian throne in 1046, becoming sole king after his co-ruler's death in 1047.

He fought years of inconclusive war against Denmark over rival claims, finally making peace in 1064 (or 1065 according to Morkinskinna) without gaining the Danish throne he sought.

He invaded England in September 1066 to press a rival claim to its throne, but was defeated and killed at the Battle of Stamford Bridge by King Harold Godwinson, days before Godwinson had to march south to face William of Normandy's invasion at Hastings.

credit.author: Zeichner: C. I. Schive, Lithograf Bucher in Bergen

works.title: Li Qingzhao
works.description:
Li Qingzhao (1084 to about 1155) was a Chinese poet of the Song dynasty, widely regarded as the greatest woman writer in the classical Chinese tradition. Her ci, a lyric verse form, moved from a settled, cultured life to loss and exile after northern China fell to invaders.

She was born in 1084 in Qi Prefecture, today's Zhangqiu in Shandong, to a literary family, and is thought to have died about 1155.

In 1101 she married Zhao Mingcheng, a scholar who shared her interest in antiquities. The Jinshi lu, a catalog of bronze and stone inscriptions, is described as her husband's work and was published after his death.

When the Jin dynasty invaded northern China in 1127, the couple fled south with part of their collection, much of which is said to have been lost along the way. Zhao Mingcheng died in 1129.

After his death she wrote an afterword to the Jinshi lu describing their marriage and their losses. She briefly remarried, with the year traditionally given as about 1132, and divorced amid scandal soon after.

Her poems, mostly short ci in personal, direct language, describe love, separation, and later grief and displacement. Only around a hundred of her poems are known to survive, out of a larger body assembled and praised by later editors.

works.title: Li Qingzhao
works.description:
Li Qingzhao (1084 to about 1155) was a Chinese poet of the Song dynasty, widely regarded as the greatest woman writer in the classical Chinese tradition. Her ci, a lyric verse form, moved from a settled, cultured life to loss and exile after northern China fell to invaders.

She was born in 1084 in Qi Prefecture, today's Zhangqiu in Shandong, to a literary family, and is thought to have died about 1155.

In 1101 she married Zhao Mingcheng, a scholar who shared her interest in antiquities. The Jinshi lu, a catalog of bronze and stone inscriptions, is described as her husband's work and was published after his death.

When the Jin dynasty invaded northern China in 1127, the couple fled south with part of their collection, much of which is said to have been lost along the way. Zhao Mingcheng died in 1129.

After his death she wrote an afterword to the Jinshi lu describing their marriage and their losses. She briefly remarried, with the year traditionally given as about 1132, and divorced amid scandal soon after.

Her poems, mostly short ci in personal, direct language, describe love, separation, and later grief and displacement. Only around a hundred of her poems are known to survive, out of a larger body assembled and praised by later editors.

works.title: Frederick Barbarossa
works.description:
Frederick I, called Barbarossa ("Redbeard"; about 1122 to 1190), was Holy Roman Emperor from 1155 until his death, and one of medieval Europe's most powerful rulers, spending much of his reign contesting control of northern Italy.

Elected King of Germany in 1152, he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor by the pope in 1155, and repeatedly invaded Italy to assert imperial authority over its wealthy independent city-states.

The Lombard League, an alliance of northern Italian cities backed by the papacy, defeated his forces at the Battle of Legnano in 1176, forcing him to recognize significant city autonomy in the Peace of Constance of 1183.

He arranged the marriage of his son Henry to Constance of Sicily, a match that later brought the Kingdom of Sicily under his family's control.

He drowned in 1190 while crossing a river in Anatolia during the Third Crusade, before reaching the Holy Land; his death caused much of his army to disband or turn back rather than continue the campaign.

works.title: Jayavarman VII
works.description:
Jayavarman VII (about 1122 to about 1218) was king of the Khmer Empire from about 1181 until his death. He drove out Cham invaders who had sacked Angkor and then led a large building program that included Angkor Thom and the Bayon.

Champa forces sacked Angkor in 1177. Jayavarman VII defeated them and was crowned about 1181; his birth and death years are estimates.

Khmer forces later brought parts of Champa under Khmer control.

He was a Mahayana Buddhist, while most earlier Khmer rulers had favored Hindu cults.

His projects include Angkor Thom, the Bayon with its towers carved with large faces, Ta Prohm (dedicated to his mother) and Preah Khan (dedicated to his father).

An inscription of 1186 at Ta Prohm credits him with 102 hospitals; the figure comes from the king's own inscriptions.

works.title: Eleanor of Aquitaine
works.medium: Church of Fontevraud Abbey Eleanor of Aquitaine effigy
works.description:
Eleanor of Aquitaine (about 1124 to 1204, with older sources giving 1122 for her birth) was successively queen of France and queen of England, and one of the wealthiest and most powerful women in 12th-century Europe as ruler of the Duchy of Aquitaine in her own right.

She inherited the vast Duchy of Aquitaine in southwestern France in 1137 and married King Louis VII of France that same year; the marriage was annulled in 1152 after producing no sons.

Weeks after the annulment she married Henry of Anjou, who became King Henry II of England in 1154, bringing her extensive French territories into the combined "Angevin Empire" that spanned much of France and England.

She supported a rebellion by three of her sons against Henry II in 1173 to 1174; after its failure, Henry kept her in confinement for about fifteen to sixteen years until his death in 1189.

Freed by her son Richard I ("the Lionheart"), she acted as regent during his crusade and captivity, and later helped secure the throne for her youngest son, John, after Richard's death in 1199.

credit.work: Church of Fontevraud Abbey Eleanor of Aquitaine effigy
credit.author: Adam Bishop

artists.lifespan: Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, about 1137–1193

works.title: Saladin
works.medium: Al-Nasir I Salah al-Din Yusuf (Saladin). AH 564-589 (1169-1193 CE) Æ Dirham (…
works.description:
Saladin (Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, about 1137 to 1193) was a Kurdish-born Muslim commander who founded the Ayyubid dynasty, ruled Egypt and much of Syria, and recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

Saladin was born about 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq, to a Kurdish family, and died in Damascus on 4 March 1193.

He rose in the service of the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din and became vizier of Fatimid Egypt in 1169.

In 1171 he ended the Fatimid Caliphate and restored Egypt's allegiance to the Abbasid caliph; his family, the Ayyubids, went on to rule Egypt and Syria.

After Nur ad-Din died in 1174 he took Damascus and brought much of Syria and northern Mesopotamia under his rule.

On 4 July 1187 his army destroyed a Crusader army at the Battle of Hattin. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187, and its Latin inhabitants could ransom themselves, though many who could not pay were enslaved.

works.title: Tamar of Georgia
works.description:
Tamar (born about 1160 or 1166, died 1213) ruled the Kingdom of Georgia from 1184 to 1213, presiding over its political and cultural high point, later called the Georgian Golden Age.

She was crowned co-ruler with her father, George III, in 1178 to secure her succession, then became sole monarch on his death in 1184, ruling with the formal title "king of kings" rather than a feminine equivalent.

Her armies won major victories against regional Muslim powers, including the Battle of Shamkor in 1195 and the Battle of Basian (dated to 1202, 1203 or 1204 depending on the source), expanding Georgian influence across much of the South Caucasus and into parts of Armenia and Anatolia.

Her reign saw significant patronage of Georgian literature and architecture, including the era's most celebrated work, Shota Rustaveli's epic poem "The Knight in the Panther's Skin," traditionally associated with her as its inspiration.

She was canonized as a saint by the Georgian Orthodox Church, and centuries of later Georgian tradition remember her reign as the kingdom's greatest period of security and cultural achievement.

works.title: Genghis Khan
works.description:
Genghis Khan (born Temujin, about 1162 to 1227) united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and founded the Mongol Empire.

He built an army based on merit and loyalty rather than clan.

His campaigns overran Central Asia, northern China, and Persia.

He promoted a written script and a legal code (the Yassa) and encouraged religious tolerance.

He died in 1227; the location of his tomb is unknown.

works.title: Razia Sultana
works.medium: Painting of Razia Sultana of the Delhi Sultanate, from the lacquer-binding co…
works.description:
Razia Sultana (about 1205 to 1240) ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240, the only woman to hold the throne in its history. She was the daughter of Iltutmish, who by tradition had named her his successor.

Razia was a daughter of the sultan Iltutmish, who reigned from 1211 to 1236. Tradition holds that he named her his heir over his sons, though he seems to have chosen Ruknuddin Firuz shortly before his death.

After Iltutmish died in 1236 her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz took the throne but was deposed within months, and Razia became sultan with the support of the people of Delhi and some nobles.

According to chroniclers she held court in public and led armies; coins were issued in her name.

She appointed Jamal ud-Din Yaqut, an Abyssinian former slave, master of the stables, a promotion Turkic nobles resented.

In 1240 Malik Altunia, the governor of Bhatinda, rebelled. She was imprisoned at Bhatinda and then married him in September 1240; they were defeated at Kaithal and killed in October 1240, and accounts differ on the details.

credit.work: Painting of Razia Sultana of the Delhi Sultanate, from the lacquer-binding cover of a manuscript of Tulsi Das' 'Ramcharitmanas', ca.1830–36

works.title: Rumi
works.description:
Rumi (Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Rumi, 1207 to 1273) was a Persian-language poet and Sufi teacher who spent his adult life in Konya, in Anatolia. His long poem, the Masnavi, and his lyric poems are among the most widely read works of Persian literature.

Rumi was born in 1207 in Balkh or nearby Wakhsh, in present-day Afghanistan or Tajikistan; sources differ. His family moved west, and he was living in Konya, in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, by about 1228.

He trained as a scholar and preacher like his father, Baha ad-Din Walad, and taught in Konya.

In 1244 he met a wandering mystic, Shams of Tabriz. Their friendship changed his life, and he began to write poetry. Shams disappeared about 1248, and accounts differ, with some saying he was killed and others that he simply moved on.

He wrote the Masnavi, a long poem in six books, and thousands of lyric poems collected in the Divan of Shams. He wrote mostly in Persian.

The Masnavi runs to some 25,000 to 27,000 couplets, with counts differing by source, composed over his last decade or so at the request of his disciple Husam al-Din Chalabi, who wrote the verses down as Rumi recited them. Some later readers called it "the Quran in Persian".

Sundiata Keita (about 1217 to 1255) is the founder of the Mali Empire, known largely from oral tradition, especially the Epic of Sundiata.

Tradition says he defeated the ruler Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina around 1235.

His story was preserved and performed by griots, hereditary oral historians.

Written sources on him are few, mainly from Arabic writers such as Ibn Khaldun.

Historians treat details of the epic with caution.

works.title: Hojo Tokimune
works.description:
Hojo Tokimune (1251 to 1284) was the eighth regent (shikken) of Japan's Kamakura shogunate, ruling as its de facto military leader during the Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281.

He became regent in 1268 at about age sixteen by Western reckoning (eighteen by traditional counting), shortly after the Mongol court of Kublai Khan first demanded Japan's submission.

He refused all Mongol diplomatic demands and reportedly had several Mongol envoys executed, a decision that made war effectively certain.

Japanese defenders repelled the 1274 and 1281 Mongol invasion fleets; in 1281 a great typhoon and, in 1274, traditionally a storm or sudden reverse wind, later remembered as kamikaze ("divine wind"), destroyed large parts of the Mongol fleets after the defenders had already inflicted losses on the invading forces.

He was a patron of Zen Buddhism, inviting the Chinese monk Wuxue Zuyuan to Kamakura and founding the temple Engaku-ji, reportedly to honor the dead of both sides after the invasions.

works.title: Amir Khusrau
works.description:
Amir Khusrau (1253 to 1325) was the leading court poet of the Delhi Sultanate, writing in Persian while drawing on the Indian world around him. He is regarded as the founding figure of Indo-Persian literature and is traditionally credited with founding qawwali, the devotional music of South Asian Sufi shrines.

Khusrau was born in 1253 near Delhi, to a Turkic father who had migrated from Central Asia and an Indian mother. He referred to this mixed heritage throughout his work.

He served as court poet under a rapid succession of Delhi sultans over more than four decades, through palace coups and dynastic changes.

He wrote in Persian, the language of the Indo-Islamic courts. His five long narrative poems, dated about 1298 to 1302, answer the Khamsa of the Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi and retell Shirin and Khusrau, Layla and Majnun, and the legend of Alexander the Great.

He was a devoted follower of the Sufi mystic Nizamuddin Auliya. Legend says Khusrau died within months of his master in 1325; their shrines stand together in Delhi.

He is traditionally credited with founding qawwali, still performed at Sufi shrines across India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Later legend also credits him with inventing the sitar and tabla, without firm historical evidence.

works.title: Giotto
works.description:
Giotto di Bondone (about 1267 to 1337) was a Florentine painter who gave medieval figures weight, emotion and space. Many call him the father of Western painting, and his frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua are his firmest work.

Giotto was born about 1267, traditionally in the Mugello valley north of Florence, though his birthplace is disputed and some recent research points to Florence itself. Vasari's story of the shepherd boy discovered by Cimabue is legend, but he was almost certainly trained in Florentine workshops.

He was traditionally credited with the Legend of St Francis frescoes at Assisi in the late 1290s, but it is now generally accepted that four different hands are identifiable there and that they came from Rome, so his authorship is doubtful; his early career is still debated.

He painted the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua about 1303 to 1305 for the banker Enrico Scrovegni. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

He worked in Rome, in Santa Croce in Florence, and at the court of King Robert of Anjou in Naples from about 1328 to 1333.

In 1334 Florence named him master of works for the cathedral, and he designed its bell tower. He died in January 1337 and was buried with public honours.

works.title: Robert the Bruce
works.medium: Medieval coin, Penny of Robert the Bruce (FindID 961323-1097387) Cropped
works.description:
Robert the Bruce (1274 to 1329) was King of Scotland from 1306 to 1329, leading Scottish resistance to English rule and securing recognition of Scottish independence shortly before his death.

He claimed the Scottish throne in 1306 after killing a rival claimant, John Comyn, in a church at Dumfries, an act that led to his excommunication by the pope.

Early in his reign he suffered several defeats and periods as a fugitive, including, according to a later popular legend, drawing perseverance from watching a spider repeatedly try to build its web.

He decisively defeated a much larger English army under Edward II at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314, the most significant Scottish military victory of the wars of independence.

The Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton in 1328 saw England formally recognize Scottish independence and Robert's kingship, a year before his death in 1329, reportedly from leprosy.

credit.work: Medieval coin, Penny of Robert the Bruce (FindID 961323-1097387) Cropped

works.title: Mansa Musa
works.medium: Catalan Atlas BNF Sheet 6 Mansa Musa (cropped)
works.description:
Mansa Musa (about 1280 to about 1337) was the ruler of the Mali Empire, famous for his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and for the great wealth of his empire.

Mali controlled major gold-producing regions of West Africa.

His pilgrimage to Mecca, with a large retinue and quantities of gold, was widely reported and reportedly disrupted the gold market in Cairo.

He supported building projects and scholarship in cities such as Timbuktu.

Sources about his life are mainly Arabic accounts and later oral tradition.

works.title: Ibn Battuta
works.medium: Handmade oil painting reproduction of Ibn Battuta in Egypt, a painting by Hip…
works.description:
Ibn Battuta (1304 to about 1369) was a Moroccan scholar and traveler whose account, the Rihla, describes journeys of about 117,000 kilometers (73,000 miles) across much of the Old World.

He left Tangier in 1325 for a pilgrimage and kept traveling for about 30 years.

He visited Arabia, East Africa, Persia, India, Southeast Asia, and the Mali Empire (1352 to 1353).

His account was dictated to the scholar Ibn Juzayy.

Historians debate whether he actually visited all of the places he describes.

credit.work: Handmade oil painting reproduction of Ibn Battuta in Egypt, a painting by Hippolyte Leon Benett.
credit.author: Léon Benett

works.title: Ibn Khaldun
works.medium: Bust of Ibn Khaldun (Casbah of Bejaia, Algeria)
works.description:
Ibn Khaldun (1332 to 1406) was a North African historian whose 'Muqaddimah' (1377) proposed a general theory of how societies and states rise and fall.

He was born in Tunis and served in several courts in North Africa and Andalusia.

He argued that group solidarity (asabiyyah) helps found dynasties, and that as rulers grow comfortable it weakens.

He wrote about economics, urban life, and the role of climate and environment.

He is sometimes called a founder of sociology and historiography.

credit.work: Bust of Ibn Khaldun (Casbah of Bejaia, Algeria)
credit.author: Reda Kerbush

works.title: Timur
works.description:
Timur (Tamerlane, traditionally dated 1336 to 1405) was a Central Asian conqueror who built the Timurid Empire and made Samarkand its centre.

Timur's birth year is contested: 1336 is the traditional date, but many contemporary accounts imply the late 1320s. He was born near Kesh (now Shahrisabz, Uzbekistan).

By about 1370 he had besieged his rival Amir Husayn at Balkh and, after Husayn's assassination, proclaimed himself sovereign of the Chagatai line of khans, with dominion over Transoxiana.

He was not a descendant of Genghis Khan and did not take the title khan. He ruled as amir through a puppet Chaghatayid khan, Suyurghatmish, and took the title güregen (royal son-in-law) through his marriage to Saray Mulk Khanum, of the Chinggisid line.

His armies campaigned in Persia, Iraq, the lands of the Golden Horde, India (Delhi was sacked in 1398), and Anatolia (he defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402).

Later chronicles describe massacres in cities he conquered. Their casualty figures are contested (see Open Questions).

works.title: Yongle Emperor
works.medium: Portrait assis de l'empereur Ming Chengzu
works.description:
The Yongle Emperor (Zhu Di; 1360 to 1424) was the third emperor of China's Ming dynasty, whose reign moved the capital to Beijing and sponsored the ocean voyages of Zheng He.

He seized the throne from his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, in a civil war from 1399 to 1402, after his father, the dynasty's founder, had passed over him in the succession.

He moved the imperial capital from Nanjing to Beijing and began construction of the Forbidden City in 1405, with most palaces completed by the end of 1417; Beijing was officially declared the principal capital in 1420.

He commissioned Zheng He's treasure-fleet voyages, six of the seven falling in his reign (the seventh came under the Xuande Emperor), the first of which departed in 1405, reaching as far as the coasts of East Africa and Arabia and projecting Ming naval power across the Indian Ocean.

He sponsored the Yongle Encyclopedia, an enormous compilation of Chinese knowledge finished in 1408 that ran to over 11,000 volumes, most of which was later lost.

works.title: Zheng He
works.description:
Zheng He (1371 to 1433) was a Chinese admiral who led seven large naval expeditions between 1405 and 1433, reaching Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa.

He served the Ming emperor Yongle and was a Muslim of Yunnan origin.

His fleets included very large ships and thousands of crew members.

The voyages displayed Ming power and collected tribute; they were then stopped.

They came decades before European ocean voyages of the same type.

works.title: Jadwiga
works.description:
Jadwiga (about 1373 to 1399) was crowned "King" of Poland in 1384 at about age ten, often described as the first woman to rule Poland in her own right, and her marriage to the Grand Duke of Lithuania began a dynastic union between the two states.

She was crowned using the male title "rex" (king) rather than "regina" (queen) to underscore that she held full sovereign authority in her own right, not merely as a royal consort.

In 1386 she married Jogaila, the pagan Grand Duke of Lithuania, who converted to Christianity and was crowned co-ruler as Wladyslaw II Jagiello, founding the Jagiellonian dynasty and beginning the Christianization of Lithuania.

She helped fund the restoration of the Krakow Academy, later the Jagiellonian University, through jewellery donated and, under her will, sold to help finance it, helping revive an institution that became a major center of learning in Central Europe.

She died in 1399, about three and a half weeks after giving birth to a daughter who also died in infancy, four days before her, ending her direct line; she was canonized by the Catholic Church in 1997.

works.title: Jan van Eyck
works.medium: Jan van Eyck - Portrait of a Man (Self Portrait?) 1433
works.description:
Jan van Eyck (born about 1380 or 1390, died 1441) was the leading painter of the Burgundian Netherlands and a founder of Early Netherlandish painting. He refined a method of thin, translucent oil glazes that let him paint light and texture with unprecedented realism.

Van Eyck was probably born sometime around 1380 or 1390 near Maaseik, in present-day Belgian Limburg. Nothing is known of his training. He appears in records about 1422 at The Hague, working for John of Bavaria.

From 1425 he was court painter and valet de chambre to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, who sent him on confidential missions, including a trip to Portugal in 1428 to 1429 to paint Princess Isabella.

About 1430 he settled in Bruges. He completed the Ghent Altarpiece, begun by his brother Hubert, in 1432, and died in Bruges in July 1441.

He did not invent oil paint, as Vasari later claimed. He built up many thin, transparent glazes, and he often signed and dated his work, sometimes with the motto Als ich can ("As I can").

Key works include the Ghent Altarpiece (1432), the Arnolfini Portrait (1434) and the Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (about 1435).

credit.work: Jan van Eyck - Portrait of a Man (Self Portrait?) 1433
credit.author: Jan van Eyck
