works.title: Ulugh Beg
works.description:
Ulugh Beg (1394 to 1449) was a Timurid ruler and astronomer who built an observatory at Samarkand and produced one of the most accurate star catalogues before the telescope.

He became governor of Samarkand in 1409, at about sixteen.

He built a madrasa (1417 to 1420) and, in 1420, an observatory.

His star catalogue, completed by about 1437, lists at least 1,018 stars.

He died in 1449 and was buried in the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum in Samarkand, beside his grandfather Timur.

works.title: Johannes Gutenberg
works.description:
Johannes Gutenberg (about 1400 to 1468) was a German metalworker who developed a movable-type printing press in Mainz around 1440 and printed the Gutenberg Bible about 1455.

He combined metal type, oil-based ink, and a press adapted from wine-making.

The 42-line Bible is the earliest major book printed from movable type in Europe.

He faced financial difficulties and lost control of his workshop to a creditor.

Printing spread rapidly across Europe within decades.

works.title: Nezahualcoyotl
works.description:
Nezahualcoyotl (1402 to 1472) was the tlatoani, or ruler, of the Acolhua city-state of Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico and a founder of the Triple Alliance with Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan. He is remembered as a lawgiver, builder and poet, though much of what is said about him comes from later writers.

Nezahualcoyotl was born in 1402 in Texcoco, the son of the ruler Ixtlilxochitl I and a Mexica princess. After the Tepanec state of Azcapotzalco conquered Texcoco and killed his father, he lived in exile.

With Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan he fought Azcapotzalco. Its defeat, traditionally dated about 1428, created the Triple Alliance. He ruled Texcoco from about 1431 until 1472, when his son Nezahualpilli succeeded him.

Later sources credit him with a law code and public works, including a dike protecting Tenochtitlan from flooding and the gardens at Tetzcotzingo.

About 34 poems are attributed to him in sixteenth-century manuscripts. Whether he composed them is debated, since "his song" can mean a song about him.

Accounts that he opposed human sacrifice and favored a single creator deity come largely from his descendant Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, writing in the early seventeenth century, and are treated with caution.

works.title: Pachacuti
works.medium: Brooklyn Museum - Pachacuti, Tenth Inca, 1 of 14 Portraits of Inca Kings (cro…
works.description:
Pachacuti (about 1418 to 1471) was the ninth Sapa Inca, under whom the Inca state expanded from a regional power into an empire.

He is credited with rebuilding Cusco and expanding Inca rule along the Andes.

Machu Picchu is believed to have been built as one of his royal estates.

He organized the state with labor obligations and roads.

Sources on him were written after the Spanish conquest and blend history and legend.

works.title: Sesshū Tōyō
works.description:
Sesshū Tōyō (1420 to 1506) was a Japanese Zen monk and painter who studied Chinese ink painting in Ming China and made it a Japanese art. He is regarded as the greatest master of Japanese ink painting.

Sesshū was born in 1420 in Bitchū Province (present-day Okayama Prefecture) and entered a Zen temple as a boy. He studied painting at Shōkoku-ji in Kyoto with the monk-painter Tenshō Shūbun.

About the 1460s he took the name Sesshū ("snow boat") and settled in Yamaguchi under the patronage of the Ōuchi family.

In 1467 he joined a trade mission to Ming China and spent about two to three years there (sources differ), travelling to Beijing and receiving an honorary title at the Tiantong monastery near Ningbo.

He returned to Japan about 1469, as the Ōnin War was tearing Kyoto apart, and worked in the provinces from his studio, the Unkoku-an, in Yamaguchi. He is credited with designing several temple gardens and died in 1506.

He painted in suibokuga, black ink and water on paper or silk, including the loose haboku ("broken ink") manner. Key works include Haboku Landscape (1495), Huike Offering His Arm to Bodhidharma (1496) and View of Ama-no-Hashidate (about 1501 to 1506).

works.title: Shen Zhou
works.medium: Shen Zhou at age 80.Palace Museum Beijing
works.description:
Shen Zhou (1427 to 1509) was a scholar-painter of Ming-dynasty China who founded the Wu School in Suzhou. He never held office, and his landscapes combine painting, poetry and calligraphy as a record of friendship and quiet life.

Shen Zhou was born in 1427 near Suzhou in the Jiangnan region, into a wealthy family of scholars, poets and collectors. His grandfather and father were painters, and the family avoided government service.

He never sat the civil service examinations. When local officials recommended him for office he declined, saying he had to care for his widowed mother, who lived to almost 100.

His home became a meeting place for Suzhou's intellectual elite, and many paintings were made as gifts for friends, marking birthdays, farewells or shared outings.

He painted "in the manner of" the four great Yuan masters, Huang Gongwang, Wu Zhen, Ni Zan and Wang Meng. Almost every painting carries his own poem in his calligraphy.

He was one of the first Chinese painters to make albums of real local places around Suzhou. Key works include Lofty Mount Lu (1467), Night Vigil (1492) and Poet on a Mountaintop (about 1500).

works.title: Matthias Corvinus
works.medium: Andrea Mantegna - King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary
works.description:
Matthias Corvinus (1443 to 1490) was King of Hungary from 1458 to 1490, a Renaissance patron-king who built one of Europe's finest libraries and modernized his kingdom's army and administration.

He was elected king at age fourteen after his father, the military commander John Hunyadi, and older brother had died, with his mother's political maneuvering and his uncle Michael Szilágyi's troops intimidating the barons securing the throne; sources differ on whether a bribe to the nobility also played a part.

He built the Black Army, a mostly mercenary standing force notable for the period, which he used to campaign against the Ottoman Empire, Bohemia, and the Holy Roman Empire, capturing Vienna in 1485.

He assembled the Bibliotheca Corviniana, described as the largest library in Europe north of the Alps and second only to the Vatican Library, employing scribes and scholars to copy classical and contemporary texts; much of it was later dispersed or destroyed after the Ottoman conquest of Hungary.

He centralized royal justice and taxation, reducing the independent power of the Hungarian nobility, though his reforms were substantially reversed by weaker successors after his death.

credit.work: Andrea Mantegna - King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary
credit.author: Andrea Mantegna

works.title: Hieronymus Bosch
works.description:
Hieronymus Bosch (about 1450 to 1516) was a painter from 's-Hertogenbosch in the Duchy of Brabant who filled his panels with hybrid monsters and crowds of tiny figures acting out human sin and folly. Only about 25 paintings are firmly attributed to him.

Bosch was born Jheronimus van Aken about 1450 in 's-Hertogenbosch. His grandfather, father and uncles were painters, and he later signed his works "Jheronimus Bosch" after the town.

Sometime between 1479 and 1481 he married Aleid Goyaerts van den Meervenne, of a wealthy family. In 1486 or 1487 he became a sworn member of the Illustrious Brotherhood of Our Blessed Lady, and he died in 1516.

He seems to have spent almost his whole life in and near 's-Hertogenbosch, and after marrying he and Aleid moved to nearby Oirschot, yet his fame spread. Philip the Handsome, Duke of Burgundy, commissioned a Last Judgment from him in 1504.

He painted in oil on oak panels, often as triptychs. Key works include The Garden of Earthly Delights (about 1495 to 1505), The Ship of Fools (about 1500 to 1510), The Temptation of St Anthony (about 1501) and the Haywain Triptych (about 1510 to 1516).

King Philip II of Spain acquired many Bosch paintings in the late 16th century, which is why the Prado in Madrid holds his greatest paintings.

Bosch was born Jheronimus van Aken about 1450 in 's-Hertogenbosch. His grandfather, father and uncles were painters, and he later signed his works "Jheronimus Bosch" after the town.

Sometime between 1479 and 1481 he married Aleid Goyaerts van den Meervenne, of a wealthy family. In 1486 or 1487 he became a sworn member of the Illustrious Brotherhood of Our Blessed Lady, and he died in 1516.

He seems to have spent almost his whole life in and near 's-Hertogenbosch, and after marrying he and Aleid moved to nearby Oirschot, yet his fame spread. Philip the Handsome, Duke of Burgundy, commissioned a Last Judgment from him in 1504.

He painted in oil on oak panels, often as triptychs. Key works include The Garden of Earthly Delights (about 1495 to 1505), The Ship of Fools (about 1500 to 1510), The Temptation of St Anthony (about 1501) and the Haywain Triptych (about 1510 to 1516).

King Philip II of Spain acquired many Bosch paintings in the late 16th century, which is why the Prado in Madrid holds his greatest paintings.

works.title: Leonardo da Vinci
works.medium: Francesco Melzi - Portrait of Leonardo (colour correction)
works.description:
Leonardo da Vinci (15 April 1452 to 2 May 1519) was an Italian painter, engineer and anatomist. He left few finished paintings, with counts differing but fewer than 25 attributed major works, some of them unfinished, including the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and thousands of notebook pages of studies.

Leonardo was born on 15 April 1452 near Vinci in Tuscany, the illegitimate son of a notary, Ser Piero, and a young woman named Caterina. He was apprenticed in Florence to Andrea del Verrocchio.

About 1482 he moved to Milan. In a letter to Duke Ludovico Sforza he stressed his skills as a military engineer before his art. In Milan he painted The Last Supper.

After the French invaded Milan in 1499 he moved between Mantua, Venice and Florence, worked briefly as a military engineer for Cesare Borgia, and in Florence began the Mona Lisa.

In 1516 King Francis I invited him to France and gave him the manor of Clos Lucé near Amboise. He died there on 2 May 1519. His pupil Francesco Melzi inherited his paintings, tools, library and personal effects, and by tradition his notebooks.

His notebooks hold thousands of pages of drawings and mirror-writing, with studies of anatomy, flight, hydraulics and optics. He dissected corpses to understand muscles and bones.

artists.lifespan: also spelled Bihzad, born about 1455–1460 and died about 1535

works.title: Behzad
works.medium: Picture of the master Behzad unknow artist
works.description:
Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād (also spelled Bihzad, born about 1455 to 1460 and died about 1535) is the most celebrated painter in the Persian tradition. He led the royal manuscript workshops at Herat and later Tabriz, and many works are attributed to him on grounds of style.

Behzād was probably born about 1455 to 1460 in Herat, capital of the Timurid dynasty founded by Timur. Orphaned young, he was brought up by the painter Mirak Naqqash, head of the royal library, and was protected by the poet and minister Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i.

Under Sultan Husayn Bayqara, who ruled Herat from 1469 to 1506, he became the leading artist of the royal kitabkhana, the library workshop. His most famous surviving works date from this period, including paintings in a Bustan of Sa'di (1488) and a Khamsa of Nizami (1494 to 1495).

After Herat fell to the Uzbeks in 1506 and then to the Safavid Shah Ismail I in about 1510, he moved to Tabriz, where in 1522 Ismail appointed him director of the royal library. He died about 1535.

A legend says that during the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 the shah hid Behzād in a cave, in some tellings together with a famous calligrapher, because he valued him more than his army.

His figures have individual faces and gestures and are often busy with everyday tasks. He often hid his signature discreetly in the architecture of a painting.

works.title: Sunni Ali
works.medium: AI illustration: A fleet of long wooden war canoes on the broad Niger river a…
works.description:
Sunni Ali (ruled about 1464 to 1492) was the ruler who turned Songhai from a small state on the Niger River into a West African empire, taking Timbuktu in 1468 as the Mali Empire declined. His birth year is unknown.

Sunni Ali became ruler of Songhai about 1464, the fifteenth in the Sunni dynasty.

He conquered Timbuktu in 1468 and, after a long siege, the trading city of Djenné, taking advantage of the weakening Mali Empire.

He was nominally Muslim but tolerated older local religious practice, and this drew tension with Muslim scholars in Timbuktu, whose chronicles remember him harshly.

He died in 1492; accounts differ on whether he drowned crossing a river or died another way.

His son Sunni Baru succeeded him but was overthrown in 1493 by Askia Muhammad, a general who accused Sunni Baru of insufficient devotion to Islam and founded a new dynasty.

works.title: Gitarja
works.description:
Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, known as Gitarja, was the third monarch of the Majapahit empire, reigning in Java from about 1328 to 1350; her birth is placed before 1309 and her death about 1372 to 1375, though both dates are uncertain.

She became queen after the assassination of her half-brother Jayanegara in 1328 (the Nagarakretagama gives 1329 for her accession), ruling in the name of her mother, Gayatri Rajapatni, who had formally retired to a Buddhist convent.

Her chief minister, Gajah Mada, is credited with a famous oath to abstain from certain pleasures until he had brought the surrounding archipelago under Majapahit's authority.

Under her reign Majapahit forces conquered Bali in 1343, defeating the kingdoms of Pejeng and Bedahulu, a major step in the empire's expansion across the Indonesian archipelago.

She stepped down in 1350 after her mother's death and was succeeded by her son, Hayam Wuruk, under whom Majapahit reached its greatest territorial extent.

works.title: Kupe
works.description:
Kupe is a legendary Polynesian navigator credited in Maori oral tradition with being the first to reach and name Aotearoa (New Zealand); no fixed historical date can be assigned to him.

Traditions describe Kupe sailing from the ancestral homeland Hawaiki, in some versions pursuing the giant octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi, and reaching the North Island of New Zealand.

He is credited with naming numerous coastal landmarks, several of which are still used today, and with returning to Hawaiki afterward to describe the land he had found.

Different iwi (tribal) traditions place him at varying points, and 19th- and 20th-century European writers synthesized these into a single traditional date of roughly 925 CE (the orthodox version tied to S. Percy Smith; other sources give about 900 to 1200 CE) that many historians now treat with caution.

No archaeological or written record fixes Kupe's voyage; the earliest confirmed archaeological evidence for human settlement of New Zealand dates to around the 13th century CE, later than most traditional accounts imply.

works.title: Montezuma II
works.description:
Montezuma II (Moctezuma; about 1466 to 1520) was the ninth ruler (tlatoani) of the Aztec Empire, reigning at its greatest territorial extent until the arrival of Hernan Cortes and the Spanish conquest.

He extended Aztec control through further conquests mainly in Oaxaca and Guerrero, plus a campaign around 1514 through the Huastec region, and reorganized the empire's tribute and administrative systems.

Cortes and a small Spanish force reached the capital Tenochtitlan in November 1519; Montezuma received them and was subsequently held as a hostage within his own palace.

Accounts of his final months differ: Spanish sources say he tried to calm his people during the fighting that followed the 1520 Toxcatl massacre and Cortes's return, and was killed by a stone thrown by his own subjects, while some later Aztec-descended chroniclers say the Spanish killed him directly.

His death in June 1520 came shortly before the Spanish were driven from the city in the "Noche Triste"; his brother Cuitlahuac and then his nephew Cuauhtemoc took up the resistance that ended with Tenochtitlan's fall in 1521.

works.title: Albrecht Dürer
works.description:
Albrecht Dürer (21 May 1471 to 6 April 1528) was a painter and printmaker from Nuremberg who brought the Italian Renaissance north. His woodcuts and engravings, sold across Europe, made him the first artist with an international reputation built largely on prints.

Dürer was born in Nuremberg, the son of a Hungarian-born goldsmith. From 1486 he was apprenticed to Michael Wolgemut, whose workshop made woodcuts for book illustration.

He travelled to Venice in 1494, and again from early 1506 to 1507, where Giovanni Bellini treated him as an equal. In 1498 he published the Apocalypse, 15 large woodcuts (some counts give 16 designs dated 1498) that made him famous.

From 1512 Emperor Maximilian I employed him and granted him a pension. On a trip to the Netherlands in 1520 to 1521 to have it confirmed by Charles V, his diary recorded his amazement at Aztec treasures sent from Mexico.

He sympathised with Martin Luther's reforms. In his last years he published treatises on measurement, fortification and human proportion.

His "AD" monogram served as a trademark, and he took action against copyists who used it.

works.title: Anacaona
works.description:
Anacaona (about 1474 to about 1504) was a Taíno cacica (chief) of Xaragua, a chiefdom in western Hispaniola, and a noted composer of ceremonial songs. She was executed by the Spanish governor Nicolás de Ovando after the killing of Taíno leaders in 1503.

Anacaona was born about 1474; her birth year is approximate. She belonged to the ruling family of Xaragua, in present-day Haiti.

She was the sister of the cacique Bohechío and the wife of Caonabo, a cacique whom the Spanish captured in 1494 or 1496, depending on the source.

After Bohechío's death about 1500 she ruled Xaragua.

Spanish sources describe her as a composer of areítos, songs that told the history of the Taíno and were performed at ceremonies.

In 1503 Governor Nicolás de Ovando came to Xaragua with soldiers. Dozens of Taíno leaders were killed at a gathering, and she was taken to Santo Domingo and executed about 1504.

works.title: Michelangelo
works.description:
Michelangelo Buonarroti (6 March 1475 to 18 February 1564) was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect and poet. His Pietà, David and Sistine Chapel paintings defined the High Renaissance, and he was the first Western artist to have a biography published in his lifetime.

Michelangelo was born at Caprese in Tuscany and grew up in Florence. At 13 he was apprenticed to Domenico Ghirlandaio, then moved to the sculpture garden of Lorenzo de' Medici, where he studied ancient statues.

The Pietà (1498 to 1499) made his name in Rome. He carved the David in Florence (1501 to 1504).

In 1505 Pope Julius II called him to Rome to design a colossal tomb, then diverted him to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508 to 1512). The unfinished tomb haunted him for decades.

In 1534 he settled permanently in Rome and painted The Last Judgment (1536 to 1541). In 1546 he became chief architect of St Peter's Basilica, and his dome became a model for later domes.

He wrote hundreds of poems, many addressed to Tommaso de' Cavalieri and Vittoria Colonna. He died in Rome, and his body was secretly taken to Florence for burial in Santa Croce.

works.title: Mimar Sinan
works.medium: 20101213 Suleymaniye Mosque Istanbul inside vertical Panorama
works.description:
Mimar Sinan (about 1489 to 1588) was chief royal architect to three Ottoman sultans for nearly fifty years. He is credited with several hundred structures, and his Selimiye Mosque at Edirne is regarded as the peak of classical Ottoman architecture.

Sinan was born about 1489 or 1490 in Ağırnas, near Kayseri in central Anatolia, into a Christian family. Sources disagree on whether it was Greek or Armenian.

He was conscripted through the devşirme levy into the Ottoman elite corps, converted to Islam and trained as a Janissary. He rose through military engineering, building bridges and fortifications on campaign for Suleiman the Magnificent.

Chelebi Lütfi Pasha appointed him chief royal architect in 1539, when he became Grand Vizier, a post Sinan held into his late nineties. He died in Istanbul in 1588.

His main buildings are the Şehzade Mosque (1543 to 1548), the Süleymaniye Mosque (1550 to 1557) and the Selimiye Mosque (1568 or 1569 to 1574 or 1575). He described them as his apprenticeship, journeyman work and masterpiece.

He worked to build domes wider and more daring than Hagia Sophia, a Byzantine cathedral converted to a mosque after 1453, using semi-domes, buttressing piers and pendentives. He also built aqueducts and bridges, some still in use.

works.title: Suleiman the Magnificent
works.description:
Suleiman the Magnificent (1494 to 1566) was Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, presiding over the empire's greatest territorial extent, military power, and legal and cultural achievement.

His armies captured Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522, then advanced deep into Central Europe, defeating and killing the King of Hungary at the Battle of Mohacs in 1526, though a first siege of Vienna in 1529 failed to take the city.

Known by the epithet Kanuni (the Lawgiver), which is absent from sixteenth and seventeenth-century Ottoman sources and may date only from the early 18th century, he issued a major legal code harmonizing Ottoman civil law with Islamic religious law across the empire's diverse territories.

His navies under admirals such as Barbarossa Hayreddin Pasha contested Mediterranean control with Spain and its allies, and Ottoman forces also pushed into Persia and Mesopotamia, capturing Baghdad in 1534.

His reign saw a major flourishing of Ottoman architecture under the chief architect Mimar Sinan, and of court poetry, painting, and decorative arts, centered on Istanbul.

works.title: Mirabai
works.medium: Kangra painting of Mirabai, the female Bhakti saint
works.description:
Mirabai (traditionally about 1498 to about 1546) was a Rajput princess from Rajasthan and one of the best-known poet-saints of the Bhakti movement, devoted to Krishna. Almost nothing about her life is documented, and the surviving poems were written down long after her time.

By tradition Mirabai was born about 1498 at Kudki in Rajasthan, into the Rathore Rajput family of Merta, and died about 1546 or 1547. Both dates come from later tradition.

Tradition says she married Bhoj Raj, heir of Mewar, in 1516, and that he died about 1521 of battle wounds.

Her poems (padas) are in Rajasthani and related Hindi, and address Krishna in the language of love and separation.

Tradition credits her with a very large number of poems. Scholars think only a few hundred may be authentic, and only two are known from manuscripts older than the early eighteenth century.

Stories that her in-laws tried to poison her, and that she vanished into an image of Krishna, are hagiographic legends. The earliest records, from the seventeenth century, do not mention her marriage or in-laws.

artists.lifespan: Malintzin, called Doña Marina by the Spanish; about 1500–about 1529

works.title: Malinche
works.description:
Malinche (Malintzin, called Doña Marina by the Spanish; about 1500 to about 1529) was a Nahua woman who served as interpreter and intermediary for Hernán Cortés during the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire in 1519 to 1521. Her dates are uncertain.

Malinche's birth is placed around 1500 and her death between about 1527 and 1529; both are estimates.

The chronicler Bernal Díaz del Castillo, writing decades later, says she was born to a noble Nahua family near Coatzacoalcos and passed into slavery as a child. This account is traditional and cannot be checked.

works.title: João III
works.description:
João III (1502 to 1557) was King of Portugal from 1521 to 1557, presiding over the height of Portugal's Asian trading empire while also introducing the Inquisition and formal colonization of Brazil.

Under his reign Portuguese trading posts and fortresses across the Indian Ocean, from East Africa to Goa, Malacca and Macau, reached their fullest extent, built on the routes opened by earlier explorers such as Vasco da Gama.

He introduced the Portuguese Inquisition in 1536, targeting Jewish converts (New Christians) suspected of secretly practicing Judaism, at the urging of factions at his court and with eventual papal approval.

He divided Brazil into hereditary captaincies from 1534 to encourage settlement and defense of the colony, a system that had mixed results and was later partly replaced by direct royal government.

He was a patron of Portuguese scholarship, moving the university at Lisbon to Coimbra in 1537, but the enormous cost of maintaining the Asian trading empire strained the crown's finances by the end of his reign.

works.title: Andrea Palladio
works.description:
Andrea Palladio (1508 to 1580) was a Renaissance architect from the Republic of Venice whose villas and churches, and an illustrated treatise, turned Roman classicism into a portable style. His influence is arguably the widest of any single architect in Western history.

Palladio was born Andrea di Pietro della Gondola in Padua in 1508. He was apprenticed to a stonemasons' guild and moved to Vicenza to work as a carver.

The nobleman Gian Giorgio Trissino gave him a classical education, renamed him "Palladio" after Pallas Athena, and took him to Rome to measure and draw ancient ruins.

His remodelling of the medieval basilica of Vicenza, dated to 1546 in some sources, made his name. For three decades he designed country villas for the Venetian nobility and churches in Venice.

In 1570 he published I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura, part treatise and part illustrated catalogue of his buildings. He died in 1580, at either Vicenza or Maser.

Key works include the Villa Rotonda (1566 to about 1592), the Teatro Olimpico (1580 to about 1585) and San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice (1566 to 1610).

works.title: Catherine de' Medici
works.medium: Catherine de Médicis - entourage de François Clouet
works.description:
Catherine de' Medici (1519 to 1589) was queen of France and, as mother to three kings, one of the most powerful figures in France during the Wars of Religion between Catholics and Huguenots.

Born into the powerful Medici banking family of Florence, she married the future Henry II of France in 1533 and became queen in 1547.

After Henry's death in 1559 she was the chief political influence for her sons Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III, though she was not formally regent under Francis II or Henry III and held the regency only for Charles IX (as gouvernante de France from December 1560 until August 1563), during a period of escalating conflict between Catholics and Protestant Huguenots.

She is widely held responsible, though the exact extent of her role is debated, for approving the assassination of Huguenot leaders, which began with the shooting of Admiral Coligny on 22 August 1572 (he survived, then was killed two days later as the massacre began) and triggered the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre in August 1572, in which about 2,000 to 3,000 Huguenots were killed in Paris and more in other cities.

She pursued marriage alliances and diplomacy across Europe to secure the Valois dynasty's position, though her efforts did not prevent the eventual extinction of the Valois line with the death of her last son in 1589.

works.title: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
works.medium: Pieter Bruegel the Elder - The Painter and the Buyer, ca. 1566 - Google Art P…
works.description:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder (about 1525 to 1569) was the most important Netherlandish painter of the 16th century. He made peasants, proverbs and the turning seasons his subjects, in crowded panels and sweeping landscapes. Only about 40 of his paintings survive.

Bruegel was probably born between 1525 and 1530, perhaps near Breda in the Duchy of Brabant. In 1551 he became a master in the painters' guild of Antwerp.

In 1552 he travelled to Italy. His drawings of the Alps on the return journey fed the mountain views of his later paintings.

In Antwerp he designed prints for the publisher Hieronymus Cock, some in the manner of Hieronymus Bosch. In 1563 he married Mayken Coecke and moved to Brussels, where he painted most of his masterpieces.

He died in Brussels in September 1569. His sons Pieter Brueghel the Younger and Jan Brueghel the Elder became successful painters and founded a dynasty.

Key works include Netherlandish Proverbs (1559), Children's Games (1560), The Tower of Babel (1563), The Hunters in the Snow (1565) and The Peasant Wedding (about 1567 to 1568).

works.title: Philip II
works.medium: Portrait of Philip II of Spain by Sofonisba Anguissola - 002b
works.description:
Philip II (1527 to 1598) was King of Spain from 1556 to 1598, ruling an empire that spanned the Iberian Peninsula, the Netherlands, parts of Italy, and vast territories in the Americas and the Philippines, which were named after him.

He inherited Spain, its Italian territories and the Spanish Americas from his father, Charles V, in 1556, and briefly held the English throne jointly through his marriage to Mary I of England from 1554 to 1558.

He directed a long, costly war to suppress a revolt in the Spanish Netherlands, beginning in 1566, that continued in various phases for decades and was never fully resolved during his reign.

He sent the Spanish Armada against England in 1588 to support a planned invasion and end English support for Dutch rebels and privateering against Spanish shipping; storms and English naval tactics destroyed much of the fleet.

He presided over Spain's peak territorial extent while also driving the crown into multiple bankruptcies, in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596, from the cost of near-constant warfare funded partly by American silver.

works.title: Sofonisba Anguissola
works.medium: Sofonisba Anguissola, Selvportræt ved staffeliet, 1556, Museum Castle in Łańcut
works.description:
Sofonisba Anguissola (about 1532 to 1629) was an Italian portrait painter from Cremona, one of the first women in Europe to build a professional career as a painter. She spent years at the Spanish court, traditionally put at about 14, and won international fame.

Sofonisba was born about 1532 in Cremona, the eldest of seven children of Amilcare Anguissola, a minor nobleman. He gave all his daughters a humanist education, and several became painters. She studied with Bernardino Campi and Bernardino Gatti.

As a noblewoman she could not study anatomy from the nude or take large public commissions, so she made portraiture her field.

Her father sent her drawings to Michelangelo, who reportedly challenged her to draw a crying boy. She answered with Boy Bitten by a Crayfish, a drawing that circulated widely.

In 1559 she was invited to Madrid to serve Queen Elisabeth of Valois, wife of Philip II, as lady-in-waiting and painting teacher. She painted the royal court for a period traditionally given as about 14 years, though sources differ, and the Spanish court arranged her marriage to a Sicilian nobleman, Fabrizio de Moncada.

After his death she married a Genoese sea captain and lived in Genoa and Palermo. In 1629 Anthony van Dyck visited her in Palermo (an earlier reading gave 1624) and recorded her advice. She died there in 1629 (older sources say 1625), in her mid-to-late nineties.

credit.work: Sofonisba Anguissola, Selvportræt ved staffeliet, 1556, Museum Castle in Łańcut

works.title: Yermak Timofeyevich
works.description:
Yermak Timofeyevich (about 1532 to 1585) was a Cossack leader whose expedition across the Urals in 1581 and 1582 overthrew the Khanate of Sibir and began the Russian conquest of Siberia. His early life is poorly known.

Yermak's birth year is uncertain; about 1532 is often given. Most accounts say he was a Volga Cossack, and some say he was wanted for piracy.

In 1581 he set out from the Ural lands of the Stroganov merchant family with several hundred men armed with firearms. Accounts of the year and the numbers vary.

In 1582 his force defeated the army of Khan Kuchum of Sibir and took the khanate's capital, Qashliq (Isker), on 26 October.

He sent word of the conquest to Tsar Ivan IV, who reportedly pardoned him and sent gifts.

Yermak died in August 1585 (some sources say 1584) in an ambush by Kuchum's forces. Tradition says he drowned in the Irtysh River, weighed down by chain mail sent by the tsar.

works.title: Lautaro
works.description:
Lautaro (about 1534 to 1557) was a Mapuche toqui, or war leader (described at Tucapel as a vice toqui under the supreme toqui Caupolicán), who organized effective resistance to Spanish conquest in what is now southern Chile, after years spent as a captured servant in the Spanish camp.

As a young captive, he served the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia and observed Spanish tactics, horsemanship and weapons before escaping back to his people.

He introduced cavalry tactics, relay messenger systems and coordinated ambushes to Mapuche warfare, adapting methods he had learned from the Spanish.

In December 1553 his forces, serving under the supreme toqui Caupolicán, defeated a Spanish column at the Battle of Tucapel, where Valdivia was captured and killed (sources differ on the details of his death), a major blow to the early Spanish conquest of Chile.

He was killed in a surprise Spanish attack on his camp at the Mataquito River in April 1557, ending a campaign that had held Spanish expansion south of the Bio-Bio River in check for years.

works.title: Akbar
works.medium: Govardhan. Akbar With Lion and Calf ca. 1630, Metmuseum (cropped)
works.description:
Akbar (1542 to 1605) was the third Mughal emperor, who took the throne as a child in 1556 and built the empire into the dominant power of the Indian subcontinent, joining military conquest to an unusual policy of religious accommodation.

Akbar was born in 1542 and became emperor in 1556 at age 13 or 14, at first guided by the regent Bairam Khan.

He expanded Mughal territory through campaigns including the capture of Chittor in 1568, and later Gujarat and Bengal, and married into Rajput ruling families as alliances.

In about 1564 (sources differ, one giving 1568) he abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims, and promoted Sulh-i Kul, "peace with all," as a governing principle.

In 1582 he introduced Din-i Ilahi, a court order drawing on several traditions, which never became a mass following and stayed largely confined to select courtiers.

His court included the historian Abul Fazl, who wrote the Akbarnama, an official chronicle of his reign.

works.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu
works.description:
Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543 to 1616) unified Japan after decades of civil war and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, a military government that ruled Japan for over two and a half centuries.

He rose through alliance and conflict with the era's other major warlords, Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, before defeating a rival coalition at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.

He was appointed shogun by the emperor in 1603, then formally passed the title to his son Hidetada in 1605 while continuing to hold real power as retired shogun until his death.

He destroyed the remaining Toyotomi family stronghold at the siege of Osaka Castle in 1615, removing the last major rival claim to national authority.

His government issued regulations restricting Christianity and foreign trade that his successors expanded into the sakoku ("closed country") policy, limiting most foreign contact for over two centuries.

works.title: Galileo Galilei
works.description:
Galileo Galilei (1564 to 1642) was an Italian scientist who used the telescope and experiments to support the Copernican view that the Earth orbits the Sun.

In 1609 and 1610 he observed the Moon's mountains and four moons of Jupiter.

He studied falling bodies and motion using experiments.

In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him and he was placed under house arrest for the rest of his life.

His 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' was published in 1632.

works.title: Caravaggio
works.description:
Michelangelo Merisi, called Caravaggio (1571 to 1610), was an Italian painter who transformed European painting around 1600 with harsh theatrical light and street-level realism. His turbulent life ended at 38, but his influence spread across Europe within a generation.

Caravaggio was born in Milan in September 1571. His name comes from the nearby town his family came from. He trained in Milan with Simone Peterzano and arrived in Rome about 1592.

Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte took him into his household. His first public commission, two large paintings of St Matthew for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi (1599 to 1600), caused a sensation. Several later altarpieces were rejected as indecorous.

Police records list brawls, assaults and insults. In 1606 he killed a man, Ranuccio Tomassoni, and fled Rome under sentence of death. He then lived in Naples, Malta and Sicily.

He died in July 1610 at Porto Ercole in Tuscany, on his way to Rome hoping for a papal pardon.

He painted directly on the canvas, apparently without preparatory drawings, from live models posed under a single strong light. His backgrounds are dark and bare (tenebrism).

works.title: Nur Jahan
works.description:
Nur Jahan (1577 to 1645) was a Mughal empress and the wife of the emperor Jahangir, who held great political power at court from about 1611 to 1627.

Nur Jahan was born Mehr-un-Nisa in 1577, the daughter of Mirza Ghiyas Beg, a Persian who served the Mughal court.

Her first husband, Sher Afghan, died in 1607. She married Jahangir in 1611 and was given the title Nur Mahal, and in 1616 Nur Jahan, "Light of the World."

As Jahangir's health declined she took a growing share of government. Coins were struck in her name, and imperial orders carried her seal.

Her father became chief minister and her brother Asaf Khan a leading noble, so her family held key posts.

She commissioned her father's tomb at Agra (1622 to 1628), an early Mughal building faced in marble with inlaid stone.

works.title: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba
works.description:
Nzinga (about 1583 to 1663) was a ruler of the kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba in present-day Angola who resisted Portuguese expansion and the slave trade for decades.

She negotiated with the Portuguese in 1622 as an ambassador for her brother.

She later took power and led resistance, including an alliance with the Dutch (1641 to 1648).

She used both diplomacy and war, and took in people escaping from slavery.

She is a symbol of resistance in Angola today.

works.title: Artemisia Gentileschi
works.medium: Self-portrait as the Allegory of Painting (La Pittura) - Artemisia Gentileschi
works.description:
Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 to about 1654) was an Italian Baroque painter, known for powerful heroines painted with Caravaggesque drama. She was the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of the Arts of Drawing.

Artemisia was born in Rome on 8 July 1593, the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, a friend and follower of Caravaggio. She trained in his workshop and painted Susanna and the Elders by the age of 17.

In 1611 she was raped by Agostino Tassi, a painter working with her father. At the seven-month trial in 1612 she was tortured with thumbscrews to test her testimony. Tassi was convicted and sentenced to exile from Rome, but the exile was never carried out and he spent less than a year in prison.

She married the Florentine painter Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence, where she won the patronage of Grand Duke Cosimo II de' Medici, befriended Galileo Galilei and in 1616 was admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. She learned to read and write in these years.

From about 1630 she settled in Naples. About 1638 she travelled to London to join her father at the court of Charles I. She is thought to have died in Naples about 1654, though some have speculated she died in the Naples plague of 1656.

She specialised in strong women from the Bible and ancient history: Judith, Susanna, Jael, Cleopatra and Lucretia. She often lent her own features to saints and allegories.

works.title: Diego Velázquez
works.medium: Diego Velázquez Autorretrato 45 x 38 cm - Colección Real Academia de Bellas A…
works.description:
Diego Velázquez (1599 to 1660) was the leading painter of Spain's Golden Age and court painter to King Philip IV for 37 years. His loose, luminous brushwork and unflattering portraits of kings, courtiers and jesters made him a "painter's painter".

Velázquez was baptised in Seville on 6 June 1599. At about 11 he entered the workshop of Francisco Pacheco, and in 1618 he married Pacheco's daughter Juana. His early Seville work shows the influence of Caravaggio.

In 1623 a portrait of the young Philip IV won him the post of court painter, and he moved to Madrid. He rose through court offices to become chamberlain of the palace.

Peter Paul Rubens, on a diplomatic mission to Madrid in 1628, encouraged him to visit Italy. His first Italian trip (1629 to 1631) transformed his colour and handling. A second (1649 to 1651) produced his portrait of Pope Innocent X.

He painted Las Meninas in 1656 and in 1659 was admitted to the noble Order of Santiago, a rare honour for a painter. He died on 6 August 1660.

He painted alla prima, often without drawing, and altered compositions on the canvas; X-rays reveal many changes of mind. His palette was restrained, built on greys, blacks and earth tones.

works.title: Rembrandt van Rijn
works.medium: Rembrandt van Rijn - Self-Portrait - Google Art Project
works.description:
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn (15 July 1606 to 4 October 1669) was the greatest artist of the Dutch Golden Age, a painter, etcher and draughtsman. His roughly 100 self-portraits form an extraordinary autobiography, from early fame and wealth to bankruptcy and loss.

Rembrandt was born in Leiden, the ninth child of a prosperous miller. He trained locally and for six months in Amsterdam with Pieter Lastman. About 1631 he moved to Amsterdam.

The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp (1632) came early in his successful career as a portraitist in the city. In 1634 he married Saskia van Uylenburgh. Three of their children died in infancy; only Titus, born 1641, survived. Saskia died in 1642, the year he completed The Night Watch.

Debts led to bankruptcy in 1656, and his house and collection were sold. He kept working. His partner Hendrickje Stoffels died in 1663 and Titus in 1668.

He died on 4 October 1669 and was buried in a rented grave in the Westerkerk.

He used chiaroscuro to direct attention and mood. His late paintings are built from thick, rough layers applied with brush, palette knife and even fingers.

credit.work: Rembrandt van Rijn - Self-Portrait - Google Art Project
credit.author: Rembrandt

works.title: Kristina of Sweden
works.medium: Swedish queen Drottning Kristina portrait by Sébastien Bourdon stor
works.description:
Kristina (1626 to 1689) was Queen of Sweden from 1632 to 1654, known for her patronage of scholars and the arts, her unexpected abdication, and her secret conversion to Catholicism in a firmly Protestant kingdom.

She became queen at age five after her father Gustavus Adolphus died in battle, ruling under a regency until she assumed full power in 1644.

She invited scholars including Rene Descartes to her court in Stockholm; Descartes died there in 1650, reportedly worn down by the early-morning hours she kept for their lessons.

She abdicated the throne in 1654 in favor of her cousin, and after leaving Sweden she converted to Catholicism in secret in Brussels in December 1654, a decision scandalous in Lutheran Sweden that she announced publicly in 1655.

She spent most of her later life in Rome under the pope's protection, becoming a prominent patron of music and art, and was one of very few women buried in St. Peter's Basilica.

credit.work: Swedish queen Drottning Kristina portrait by Sébastien Bourdon stor
credit.author: Sébastien Bourdon

works.title: Christopher Wren
works.description:
Christopher Wren (1632 to 1723) was an English mathematician and astronomer, a founder of the Royal Society, who became an architect after the Great Fire of London in 1666. He designed more than fifty City churches and a new St Paul's Cathedral, topped out in 1708 and declared complete by Parliament in 1711.

Wren was born in East Knoyle, Wiltshire, the son of a clergyman. He was appointed professor of astronomy at Gresham College at 25, then Savilian Professor of Astronomy at Oxford, and was a founding member of the Royal Society in 1662.

His architectural career began with the Sheldonian Theatre in Oxford. The Great Fire of September 1666 destroyed old St Paul's and most of the City.

He was appointed Surveyor of the King's Works in 1669 and spent the rest of his working life on the City's parish churches and on St Paul's. He died in 1723, aged 90, and is buried in the cathedral crypt.

He combined the classical vocabulary of Inigo Jones and Palladio with French and Italian Baroque elements he studied on a research trip to Paris, the only time he travelled outside England.

The dome of St Paul's is three independent shells nested inside one another, so that exterior profile, interior ceiling and structural core could each be optimised separately.

works.title: Johannes Vermeer
works.description:
Johannes Vermeer (1632 to 1675) was a painter of Delft in the Dutch Republic. About 35 paintings are accepted as his, mostly quiet interiors lit by daylight from a window. Almost forgotten for 200 years after his death, he is now among the most famous painters in the world.

Vermeer was baptised in Delft on 31 October 1632. His father was a silk weaver who also dealt in art and ran an inn. Nothing is known of Vermeer's training.

In 1653 he married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic from a wealthier family, and probably converted. The same year he joined Delft's Guild of St Luke, which later elected him one of its leaders several times.

The couple lived with Catharina's mother and had 15 children, 11 of whom survived. He also worked as an art dealer, and his slow output was bought largely by one local patron, Pieter van Ruijven.

In 1672, the Dutch Republic's "Disaster Year", France invaded and the art market collapsed. He died in 1675, aged 43, leaving his family deep in debt.

He used costly natural ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli, even in shadows. Key works include The Milkmaid (about 1657 to 1658), View of Delft (about 1660 to 1661) and Girl with a Pearl Earring (about 1665).

works.title: Isaac Newton
works.description:
Isaac Newton (1642 to 1727) was an English mathematician and physicist whose laws of motion and universal gravitation formed the basis of classical mechanics.

His 'Principia' (1687) presents the laws of motion and the law of gravitation.

He developed calculus, independently of Leibniz, leading to a priority dispute.

He studied optics, showing that white light is composed of colors.

He also spent much time on alchemy and theology.

artists.name: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
artists.short_name: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

works.title: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
works.description:
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (born 1648 or 1651, died 1695) was a nun, poet and playwright in colonial Mexico City. She is regarded as one of the leading Spanish-language writers of the seventeenth century and an early defender of women's right to study.

Juana Ramírez de Asbaje was born at San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City. Baptismal records point to 1648 or 1651, and the year is debated. She died on 17 April 1695.

Largely self-taught, she served at the viceroy's court in her teens and in 1669 entered the Hieronymite convent of San Jerónimo.

She wrote lyric poems, plays such as Los empeños de una casa (1683) and the long poem Primero sueño. Her first collection, Inundación castálida, was printed in Madrid in 1689.

In 1690 the Bishop of Puebla published her critique of a sermon by António Vieira as the Carta atenagórica and, writing as "Sor Filotea," urged her toward religious study. She answered in 1691 with the Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz, defending women's right to learn.

In 1693 and 1694 she stopped writing and signed penitential documents. Whether she sold her library or had it taken, and how far the choice was hers, is debated.

works.title: Peter the Great
works.medium: Inconnu d'après J.-M. Nattier, Portrait de Pierre Ier (musée de l’Ermitage)
works.description:
Peter I, called Peter the Great (1672 to 1725), ruled Russia from 1682, jointly at first and alone from 1696, until 1725, driving a sweeping program of westernizing reform and transforming Russia into a major European power.

He traveled incognito through Western Europe in 1697 to 1698 on the "Grand Embassy," working for a time as a shipwright in the Netherlands to study European shipbuilding and technology firsthand.

He fought a long war against Sweden, the Great Northern War from 1700 to 1721, winning a decisive victory at the Battle of Poltava in 1709 and gaining territory on the Baltic Sea that made Russia a major naval power.

He founded the city of St. Petersburg in 1703 on newly won Baltic territory, building it as a planned European-style capital and moving the seat of government there from Moscow.

He reorganized the Russian government, military, and church administration along Western European lines, and required Russian nobles to adopt Western dress, in a well-known instance personally cutting off boyars' traditional long beards to symbolize the change.

works.title: Jeong Seon
works.medium: Jeong Seon-Taking a reast after reading books-d1
works.description:
Jeong Seon (1676 to 1759), pen name Gyeomjae, was a Korean painter of the Joseon dynasty who transformed landscape painting by depicting the real scenery of Korea instead of imagined Chinese scenery. His "true-view landscape" (jingyeong sansuhwa) expressed a growing pride in Korean culture.

Jeong Seon was born in 1676 in Hanyang (modern Seoul), into a scholarly family of modest means. His father died when he was young. He trained in painting and in Neo-Confucian learning.

Through recommendations he held government posts, including county magistrate at Hayang and Yangcheon, and rose to high official rank in old age.

He lived near Mount Inwang in Seoul. His friend the poet Yi Byeong-yeon exchanged poems and paintings with him for decades.

In 1711 and 1712 he travelled to the Diamond Mountains (Geumgangsan), and the albums he made there made his name. He died in 1759 at 83.

For centuries Korean painters had followed Chinese models. He painted the actual scenery of Korea and invented his own brushstrokes: sharp vertical strokes for granite peaks and soft wet dots for forested earth mountains.

works.title: Vitus Bering
works.description:
Vitus Bering (1681 to 1741) was a Danish-born officer in the Russian navy who led two expeditions across Siberia to chart the waters between Asia and North America. The strait and sea between the continents carry his name.

Bering was baptized on 5 August 1681 in Horsens, Denmark, and joined the Russian navy in 1704 under Peter the Great. He died on 19 December 1741 on the island now named for him.

On the First Kamchatka Expedition (1725 to 1730) he sailed through the strait between Siberia and Alaska in 1728 without sighting the American coast, though some historians think it was visible.

The Great Northern Expedition (1733 to 1743) grew to about 3,000 people, one of the largest scientific undertakings of its time.

In 1741 his ship, the St. Peter, and a second ship under Aleksei Chirikov, the St. Paul, sailed separately toward America. Chirikov's crew sighted land about a day earlier, on 15 July by the dates given in the sources; Bering's crew sighted Mount Saint Elias on 16 July.

On the return voyage the St. Peter wrecked on an uninhabited island. Bering died there, a death traditionally put down to scurvy and exposure, though a 1991 analysis of his remains judged heart failure the likely cause; of 77 men aboard, 46 survived to reach Kamchatka the next year.

credit.author: Институт Археологии РАН (Institute of Archaeology in Russian Academy of Sciences )

works.title: Vitus Bering
works.description:
Vitus Bering (1681 to 1741) was a Danish-born officer in the Russian navy who led two expeditions across Siberia to chart the waters between Asia and North America. The strait and sea between the continents carry his name.

Bering was baptized on 5 August 1681 in Horsens, Denmark, and joined the Russian navy in 1704 under Peter the Great. He died on 19 December 1741 on the island now named for him.

On the First Kamchatka Expedition (1725 to 1730) he sailed through the strait between Siberia and Alaska in 1728 without sighting the American coast, though some historians think it was visible.

The Great Northern Expedition (1733 to 1743) grew to about 3,000 people, one of the largest scientific undertakings of its time.

In 1741 his ship, the St. Peter, and a second ship under Aleksei Chirikov, the St. Paul, sailed separately toward America. Chirikov's crew sighted land about a day earlier, on 15 July by the dates given in the sources; Bering's crew sighted Mount Saint Elias on 16 July.

On the return voyage the St. Peter wrecked on an uninhabited island. Bering died there, a death traditionally put down to scurvy and exposure, though a 1991 analysis of his remains judged heart failure the likely cause; of 77 men aboard, 46 survived to reach Kamchatka the next year.

works.title: Tupaia
works.medium: A Maori man and Joseph Banks exchanging a crayfish for a piece of cloth, c. 1769
works.description:
Tupaia (about 1725 to 1770) was a priest and navigator from Ra'iatea in the Society Islands who sailed with James Cook on the Endeavour in 1769 and drew a chart of Pacific islands. He died at Batavia in 1770.

Tupaia was born about 1725 on Ra'iatea and became a priest and navigator. After warriors from Borabora took Ra'iatea, he took refuge on Tahiti.

In July 1769 he joined Cook's Endeavour, usually said to be at Tahiti (sources differ on the place), as a guide and interpreter, with a young servant, Taiata.

In August 1769 he began a chart of the Pacific with Cook, Joseph Banks and other officers. Sources differ: it is said to show about 130 islands, of which he could name about 74, and it is often described as centered on Ra'iatea.

The chart did not match European map conventions, and modern scholars have argued that it follows a Polynesian way of organizing islands by voyages and directions.

On reaching New Zealand in October 1769 he could speak with Māori, whose language is closely related to Tahitian, and he interpreted for the crew.

artists.name: Ajuricaba
artists.region: Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands

works.title: Ajuricaba
works.medium: Americo Makk, Portait of Chief Ajuricaba
works.description:
Ajuricaba (died about 1727) was a leader of the Manaos people of the Rio Negro, in the Brazilian Amazon, who resisted Portuguese colonization and the enslavement of Indigenous people in the 1720s. Almost everything known about him comes from Portuguese sources.

Ajuricaba led the Manaos (Manaó) people of the Rio Negro valley, in present-day Amazonas, Brazil. His birth year and origins are unclear; the date given here is that of his death.

He resisted Portuguese colonization and the enslavement of Indigenous people in the 1720s. Portuguese accounts say he allied with Dutch traders from the Guianas, who were rivals of Portugal.

The governor of Grão-Pará, João da Maia da Gama, sent forces against him. Some accounts say he was captured through the betrayal of allies.

Portuguese accounts say that while he was being taken in chains toward Belém, he and his men rose against their guards, and he threw himself into the river and drowned, in 1727 (some sources say 1728).

He is remembered in Brazil as a symbol of Indigenous resistance. The city of Manaus takes its name from the Manaos people.

credit.work: Americo Makk, Portait of Chief Ajuricaba
credit.author: Americo Makk

artists.name: Túpac Amaru II
artists.lifespan: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, born 1738 or about 1742, died 1781

works.title: Túpac Amaru II
works.medium: Acuarela de Túpac Amaru II crop
works.description:
Túpac Amaru II (José Gabriel Condorcanqui, born 1738 or about 1742, died 1781) was a hereditary Indigenous chief and trader who led a large rebellion against Spanish colonial rule in the Andes in 1780 and 1781. He was executed in Cusco.

José Gabriel Condorcanqui was born in 1738 (some sources say about 1742) in the highlands near Cusco. He became a kuraka (hereditary local chief) and a successful muleteer and trader.

He took the name Túpac Amaru, claiming descent from the Inca ruler Túpac Amaru, whom the Spanish executed in 1572.

Grievances behind the rebellion included higher Spanish taxes, forced sales of goods to Indigenous communities, and the mita, forced labor in mines.

On 4 November 1780 he seized a local Spanish official, Antonio de Arriaga, who was executed shortly after (10 November 1780 per two sources), which began the rebellion.

He issued proclamations ending the mita and other abuses, and the rebellion spread across the southern highlands.

credit.author: Anonymous Unknown author

works.title: Basawan
works.medium: A Court Scene, Folio from a Manuscript of Sadi's Gulistan (Rose Garden) LACMA…
works.description:
Basawan was a Hindu painter in the imperial workshop of the Mughal emperor Akbar, active from about 1560 to about 1600, though he is described as flourishing between 1580 and 1600 and the earlier date rests on his earliest mention, in a Tutinama of about 1556 to 1561. His birth and death dates are unknown, so the dates here mark his period of activity. Akbar's historian ranked him among the best of the workshop's more than a hundred painters.

Almost nothing is known of Basawan's life beyond his paintings and a brief praise in Abu'l-Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari. He was a Hindu and probably joined the imperial workshop as a young man in the 1560s. His earliest mention is in an illustrated Tutinama of about 1556 to 1561, and he is described as flourishing between 1580 and 1600.

Akbar reigned from 1556 to 1605. The workshop's Persian masters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, had trained in the tradition of Behzād and directed Indian artists in producing vast illustrated manuscripts, among them the Hamzanama, 1,400 large paintings.

Abu'l-Fazl praised his skill in composition, faces, colour and portraiture, and wrote that many critics preferred him even to the celebrated Daswanth.

His name is written in the margins of paintings in the Razmnama (a Persian translation of the Mahabharata), the Darabnama, the Akbarnama and small books of Persian poetry made in Lahore in the 1590s. In large history manuscripts he often designed the composition and another artist added the colour.

From 1580 Jesuit missionaries brought European engravings and paintings to Akbar's court. He studied them closely, adapting their shading and deep space, and was among the first Indian painters to absorb European modelling and perspective.

works.title: Queen Amina of Zazzau
works.medium: AI illustration: The walled gates and ramparts of a fortified hausa city at dusk
works.description:
Queen Amina of Zazzau is a traditional figure said to have ruled Zazzau (Zaria), a Hausa state in present-day northern Nigeria, for about 34 years around the turn of the 16th and 17th centuries. She is known from later tradition, and her dates and status are disputed.

Some sources give Amina's reign as 1576 to 1610; her birth and death years are uncertain (some accounts give 1533 and 1610), and the dates here are those of the reign. Whether she held the title of queen is disputed, and she does not appear on the regnal lists. Some scholars instead place her in the early to mid fifteenth century, because the Kano Chronicle calls her a contemporary of Muhammad Dauda, who ruled from 1421 to 1438.

Much of what is known comes from the Kano Chronicle, a late 19th-century compilation of older oral tradition, and from Muhammad Bello's history Infaq al-Maysur (dated to 1812 or to about 1836, sources differ), written more than two centuries later.

Tradition says she led Zazzau's army, expanded its territory, and increased its wealth through control of trade routes.

Earthen walls around Hausa towns are traditionally attributed to her.

Scholars generally accept that she existed, but the details of her life come from tradition.

works.title: Queen Suriyothai
works.description:
Queen Suriyothai was a consort of King Maha Chakkraphat of the Ayutthaya kingdom, in present-day Thailand, traditionally said to have died in 1548 defending her husband on elephant-back during a Burmese invasion. Her birth year is traditionally given as 1511, and her story rests on Siamese chronicles alone.

She was a consort of Maha Chakkraphat, who became king of Ayutthaya in 1546 or 1548, as sources differ.

In 1548 the Burmese king Tabinshwehti invaded Ayutthaya. Siamese chronicles say Suriyothai, disguised and riding an elephant, placed herself between her husband and an enemy commander and was killed by his blow.

No Burmese chronicle records this episode, and her historicity is questioned. Thai accounts add that her daughter, Princess Boromdilok, was also mortally wounded.

A memorial stupa, the Chedi Si Suriyothai, was built by Maha Chakkraphat at Wat Suan Luang Sopsawan on the bank of the Chao Phraya near Ayutthaya, and is traditionally associated with the site of her death.

Thai nationalist commemoration of her grew in the twentieth century, including a widely seen 2001 film.

works.title: Francisco Goya
works.medium: Vicente López Portaña - el pintor Francisco de Goya
works.description:
Francisco Goya (30 March 1746 to 16 April 1828) was a Spanish court painter and printmaker, often called the last of the Old Masters and the first of the moderns. Illness, political repression and the Napoleonic invasion drove him from brilliant royal portraits toward satire, violence and the irrational.

Goya was born in Fuendetodos in Aragon and grew up in Zaragoza. In 1773 he married Josefa Bayeu, sister of the court painter Francisco Bayeu, who helped him win work designing tapestry cartoons in Madrid. By 1786 he was painter to the king, and in 1799 First Court Painter to Charles IV.

In 1792 to 1793 an illness left him permanently deaf. In 1799 he published Los Caprichos, satirical etchings mocking superstition and the clergy.

When Napoleon's armies invaded Spain in 1808 he witnessed atrocities on both sides and recorded them in The Disasters of War, prints published only 35 years after his death. He painted The Second and Third of May 1808 in 1814.

Disillusioned by the repressive rule of Ferdinand VII, he retreated to a house outside Madrid and covered its walls with the Black Paintings, including Saturn Devouring His Son (1819 to 1823). In 1824 he went into exile in Bordeaux, where he died.

His portraits, influenced by Velázquez, use loose brushwork and avoid flattery. He mastered aquatint for deep shadows and later applied paint with knives, rags and fingers.

credit.work: Vicente López Portaña - el pintor Francisco de Goya
credit.author: Vicente López Portaña

works.title: Kamehameha I
works.medium: Louis Choris (1795-1828) - Kamehameha, King of the Sandwich Islands by Louis …
works.description:
Kamehameha I (about 1750 to 1819) was a chief of Hawaiʻi Island who united the Hawaiian Islands under one rule by 1810, founding the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, whose last monarch was Liliuokalani.

Kamehameha was born at Kohala on Hawaiʻi Island. Estimates of his birth year range from 1736 to 1761. He died on 8 May 1819, though some sources say 14 May.

After his uncle, the ruler Kalaniʻōpuʻu, died in 1782, he became guardian of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku and defeated his cousin Kīwalaʻō at the Battle of Mokuʻōhai, gaining Hawaiʻi Island after years of war.

He used Western firearms and cannon and advisers such as John Young and Isaac Davis. In 1795 he invaded Oʻahu, and at Nuʻuanu hundreds of defenders were driven over the Pali cliff.

In 1810 Kauaʻi and Niʻihau came under his authority by negotiation with their ruler Kaumualiʻi, who stayed on as a tributary king.

The Law of the Splintered Paddle (Māmalahoe Kānāwai), protecting noncombatants, is said to come from a 1782 incident in which fishermen struck him with a paddle.

works.title: Usman dan Fodio
works.description:
Usman dan Fodio (1754 to 1817) was a Fulani scholar and religious leader who led the jihad that created the Sokoto Caliphate.

He taught and preached in the Hausa state of Gobir and wrote widely in Arabic and Fulfulde.

In 1804 he and his followers left Gobir, and the jihad began in February of that year.

He is regarded as the founder of the Sokoto Caliphate and its first sultan or caliph.

His brother and his son helped to administer the new state.

works.title: Katsushika Hokusai
works.description:
Katsushika Hokusai (1760 to 1849) was a Japanese ukiyo-e artist from Edo, creator of The Great Wave off Kanagawa. He produced paintings, book illustrations and, in his seventies, the landscape print series that made him world-famous.

Hokusai was born in 1760 in the Katsushika district of Edo (modern Tokyo). As a teenager he worked in a lending library and trained as a woodblock carver. About 18 he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō.

He changed his artistic name more than 30 times and is said to have moved house more than 90 times. He lived in poverty for much of his life. His daughter Katsushika Ōi became a fine painter and assisted him in his old age.

In 1814 he began publishing the Hokusai Manga, fifteen volumes of sketches. About 1830 to 1832 he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, which includes The Great Wave off Kanagawa (about 1831).

In the postscript to One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji (1834) he wrote that nothing he drew before age 70 was worth noticing. He died in Edo on 10 May 1849, at 88, reportedly saying that with five more years he could have become a true painter.

Ukiyo-e was a collaborative art: he drew the design, specialist carvers cut it into blocks, one for each colour, and printers pressed the paper by hand. The Fuji series used the newly imported Prussian blue pigment.

works.title: Sequoyah
works.medium: Henry Inman - Sequoyah - Google Art Project
works.description:
Sequoyah (about 1770 to 1843) was a Cherokee silversmith who created the Cherokee syllabary, a writing system for the Cherokee language, completed by 1821. It is one of the few writing systems whose invention by a single known person is well documented.

Sequoyah was born about 1770 in the Cherokee town of Tuskegee, in present-day Tennessee; the birth year is approximate.

He did not read or write English. He began work on a writing system for Cherokee about 1809 and completed it by 1821.

The syllabary has 85 characters (86 in early versions), each standing for a syllable.

The system spread rapidly among the Cherokee. The Cherokee Phoenix, a newspaper printed in Cherokee and English, began publication in 1828 and was the first Native newspaper in the United States.

He later lived among Cherokee who had moved west of the Mississippi River. He died in August 1843 in Mexico while searching for a group of Cherokee said to have settled there.

credit.work: Henry Inman - Sequoyah - Google Art Project
credit.author: Henry Inman

works.title: J. M. W. Turner
works.description:
Joseph Mallord William Turner (April 1775 to 19 December 1851) was the greatest British landscape painter and a bold colourist. He began as a precise topographical watercolourist, and his late paintings dissolve ships, trains and cities into light, mist and weather.

Turner was born in Covent Garden, London, the son of a barber and wigmaker. At 14 he entered the Royal Academy Schools and at 15 exhibited his first watercolour. He was elected a full Royal Academician in 1802, at 26 or 27 depending on the source.

He travelled tirelessly in Britain, the Alps, France, Germany and Italy, especially Venice, filling hundreds of sketchbooks.

He never married but had two daughters with Sarah Danby. John Ruskin championed him in Modern Painters (1843). He died in Chelsea and was buried in St Paul's Cathedral.

By the 1830s he painted natural forces themselves, storms, fire, sunlight and steam. He worked thin washes over white grounds, scraped and rubbed his canvases, and applied paint thickly with knives.

He painted steamships and railways alongside Venetian lagoons. Rain, Steam and Speed (1844) is one of the first great paintings of modern technology.

works.title: Jane Austen
works.description:
Jane Austen (1775 to 1817) was an English novelist whose six completed novels of courtship, inheritance and class anxiety among the gentry remain among the most widely read in the language. All were published anonymously in her lifetime.

Austen was born in 1775 in Steventon, Hampshire, the seventh of eight children of a country clergyman, in a family that encouraged reading, amateur theatre and writing.

Sense and Sensibility appeared in 1811, credited only to "A Lady", followed by Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814), Emma (1815) and, after her death, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion (1817).

Only close family knew of her authorship. She fell ill, probably with Addison's disease though the cause is debated, and died in 1817 at 41. Her authorship was publicly acknowledged in a biographical notice her brother attached to her last two novels.

She worked within a deliberately narrow social canvas, mainly the English gentry, courtship, income and inheritance, rather than the wider political events of her era.

Her distinctive technique is free indirect discourse: narrating in the third person while letting the prose absorb a character's own irony or blind spots, so the reader senses a character's error before the character does.

works.title: Simón Bolívar
works.medium: Simón Bolívar. Toro Moreno, Luis. 1922, Legislative Palace, La Paz
works.description:
Simón Bolívar (1783 to 1830) was a Venezuelan military and political leader who led the independence of several South American countries from Spain and tried to unite them as Gran Colombia.

He was born in Caracas to a wealthy family.

He and Sucre led the campaigns that freed present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia.

He met José de San Martín at Guayaquil in 1822.

Gran Colombia split apart within seven years, and Bolívar died in 1830.

credit.work: Simón Bolívar. Toro Moreno, Luis. 1922, Legislative Palace, La Paz
credit.author: Luis Enrique Toro Moreno (1897-1933)

works.title: Shaka
works.description:
Shaka kaSenzangakhona (about 1787 to 1828) was the founder of the Zulu Kingdom, who transformed its military and political organization.

He came to power around 1816 and expanded the Zulu state quickly.

He is credited with new weapons and tactics, including the short stabbing spear and a 'buffalo horns' formation.

He was assassinated in 1828 by his half-brothers.

Much of what is told about him comes from colonial-era European accounts and oral tradition, and is debated.

works.title: Sacagawea
works.medium: Detail Lewis & Clark at Three Forks
works.description:
Sacagawea (about 1788 to 1812, or by another account 1884) was a young woman of disputed Shoshone or Hidatsa birth who traveled with the Lewis and Clark expedition from 1804 to 1806 as an interpreter, and later became one of the most commemorated women in the United States.

Sacagawea was born about 1788, by tradition among the Lemhi Shoshone in present-day Idaho, though some recent work argues she was born Hidatsa.

About 1800 she was taken by a Hidatsa raiding party. As a teenager she married the trader Toussaint Charbonneau, and her son Jean Baptiste was born on 11 February 1805.

Charbonneau and Sacagawea joined the Lewis and Clark expedition at Fort Mandan in 1804. In August 1805 she met her brother Cameahwait, a Shoshone leader, whose horses the party needed to cross the Rockies.

Historians describe her chiefly as an interpreter and a sign of peaceful intent, more than a guide, though she gave directions in a few places.

A fur-trade clerk recorded in 1812 that Charbonneau's wife had died, but Shoshone oral tradition holds she lived until 1884 on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming. Historians disagree.

credit.work: Detail Lewis & Clark at Three Forks
credit.author: Edgar Samuel Paxson

works.title: Utagawa Hiroshige
works.description:
Utagawa Hiroshige (1797 to 1858) was the last great master of the ukiyo-e woodblock print, a lyrical designer of rain, snow, moonlight and travellers on the road. His series on the Tōkaidō highway and on Edo were huge commercial successes and later inspired European artists.

Hiroshige was born in Edo in 1797 into the Andō samurai family, whose hereditary job was fire warden at Edo Castle. Both parents died when he was about 12, and he inherited the post.

About 1811 he became a pupil of the print designer Utagawa Toyohiro, who gave him the name Hiroshige. He handed the fire warden post to his son in 1823 and turned to landscape after Hokusai's Fuji series opened a new market.

According to tradition he travelled the Tōkaidō in 1832 with an official delegation. The prints he published in 1833 to 1834 made him the most popular landscape artist in Japan.

In 1856 he became a Buddhist monk but kept working on One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. He died in Edo on 12 October 1858, probably in a cholera epidemic.

He designed the prints; carvers and printers made them. He used soft colour gradations (bokashi) and, in the Edo series, a vertical format with a large foreground object framing a distant view. "Hiroshige blue" was made with imported Prussian blue.

works.title: Charles Darwin
works.description:
Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) was an English naturalist who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection, published in 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859.

His voyage on HMS Beagle (1831 to 1836) gave him observations that led to his theory.

Alfred Russel Wallace independently reached the same idea, and the two announced it together in 1858.

'The Descent of Man' (1871) applied the theory to human origins.

Modern genetics later provided the mechanism of inheritance that Darwin lacked.

works.title: Truganini
works.medium: Black Man's Cove John Skinner Prout
works.description:
Truganini (about 1812 to 1876) was a Tasmanian Aboriginal woman of the Nuenonne people who grew up on Bruny Island and lived through the British colonization of Tasmania and died in Hobart. She was later widely called "the last Tasmanian Aboriginal," a label that Tasmanian Aboriginal people reject.

Truganini was born about 1812, reportedly at Recherche Bay in southern Tasmania, as a member of the Nuenonne people, and she grew up on Bruny Island.

Accounts say members of her family were killed or abducted by colonists during the Black War of the 1820s and early 1830s.

In the 1830s she worked with George Augustus Robinson, a government-appointed conciliator who persuaded surviving Aboriginal people to move to Flinders Island, where disease and hardship were severe.

She later lived at Oyster Cove, south of Hobart, and died on 8 May 1876.

Her skeleton was exhumed in 1878 and displayed in the Tasmanian Museum from 1904 until 1947, despite her reported fear of mutilation.

works.title: Ada Lovelace
works.medium: Ada Lovelace daguerreotype by Antoine Claudet 1843 - cropped
works.description:
Ada Lovelace (1815 to 1852) was an English mathematician who wrote extensive notes on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, including what is often regarded as the first published computer algorithm.

She was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron.

Her 1843 notes described how the engine could compute a sequence of Bernoulli numbers.

She suggested that such a machine might manipulate symbols beyond numbers, such as music.

The extent of her original contribution versus Babbage's is debated.

credit.work: Ada Lovelace daguerreotype by Antoine Claudet 1843 - cropped
credit.author: Antoine Claudet

works.title: Queen Victoria
works.description:
Victoria (1819 to 1901) was Queen of the United Kingdom from 1837 to 1901, the longest-reigning British monarch until Elizabeth II, presiding over a period of industrial growth and imperial expansion later named after her.

She became queen at eighteen after the death of her uncle William IV, and married her cousin Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha in 1840, with whom she had nine children who married into royal families across Europe.

Her reign saw Britain's industrial economy expand rapidly and its colonial empire grow substantially, and she was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876.

After Albert's death in 1861 she withdrew from public life for years, a long seclusion that made her briefly unpopular before she gradually resumed public duties.

Constitutional practice during her reign shifted royal power further toward a largely ceremonial role exercised through elected ministers, even as the monarchy's cultural and symbolic prominence grew.

works.title: Harriet Tubman
works.description:
Harriet Tubman (about 1822 to 1913) was an American abolitionist who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then guided others to freedom on the Underground Railroad. She later served the Union Army in the Civil War.

Tubman was born Araminta Ross into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland; her birth year is uncertain, with sources giving dates from 1815 to 1825 and about 1822 the most favoured.

As a teenager she suffered a severe head injury when an overseer threw a metal weight, and had seizures and headaches for the rest of her life.

She escaped to Pennsylvania in 1849 and afterward made about 13 trips back to Maryland, guiding roughly 70 people to freedom, according to her biographers.

During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a cook, nurse, scout and spy. In June 1863 she helped guide the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people, though some sources give more than 750.

After the war she lived in Auburn, New York, where she cared for her family and for elderly people, and she worked for women's suffrage.
