artists.region: Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands

works.title: Pedro II
works.description:
Pedro II (1825 to 1891) was Emperor of Brazil from 1831 to 1889, presiding over six decades of relative political stability, territorial integrity, and gradual abolition of slavery before being deposed in a republican coup.

He became emperor at age five after his father abdicated, ruling under regents until being declared of age early, in 1840, to stabilize a period of regional revolts.

His government fought the Paraguayan War from 1864 to 1870 alongside Argentina and Uruguay, the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history, which devastated Paraguay's population.

He personally supported gradual abolition of slavery, and his daughter and regent, Princess Isabel, signed the Golden Law abolishing slavery outright in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so.

Brazilian military officers, landowners angered by abolition, and republican advocates combined to depose him in a bloodless coup in November 1889, ending the monarchy and sending him into exile in Europe, where he died in 1891.

credit.author: Mathew Benjamin Brady / Levin Corbin Handy

works.title: Leo Tolstoy
works.description:
Leo Tolstoy (1828 to 1910) was a Russian novelist, author of the realist epics War and Peace and Anna Karenina. A religious crisis in the second half of his life turned him toward shorter fiction and writing on faith, mortality and nonviolence that influenced Gandhi.

Tolstoy was born in 1828 into an aristocratic family at Yasnaya Polyana, the estate south of Moscow he inherited and managed for most of his life. He served briefly as an army officer in the Crimean War.

In the 1860s and 1870s he wrote War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1877), and founded a school for the children on his estate.

After Anna Karenina he underwent a spiritual crisis, described in A Confession. He rejected the Russian Orthodox Church, embraced an ascetic, pacifist reading of Christian ethics and increasingly disowned his earlier fiction as morally frivolous.

His later works include The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886), The Kreutzer Sonata (1889) and Resurrection (1899), shorter, starker and more didactic than the novels.

War and Peace argues in long digressions that the forces driving historical events lay far beyond the control of any single general or emperor.

works.title: Rani Lakshmibai
works.description:
Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi (about 1828 to 1858) was an Indian queen who became a leader of the 1857 rebellion and a national symbol of resistance.

She ruled Jhansi as regent after her husband's death, and the British refused to recognize her adopted heir.

She led the defense of Jhansi against British forces in 1858.

She and other rebels seized the fortress of Gwalior on 1 June 1858.

She died in battle on 17 June 1858.

works.title: Savitribai Phule
works.medium: Savitribai Phule statue, Maharashtra sadan, New Delhi
works.description:
Savitribai Phule (1831 to 1897) was an Indian educator, poet and social reformer in Maharashtra who, with her husband Jyotirao Phule, opened one of the first schools for girls in Pune in 1848. She died of plague in 1897 after nursing patients.

Savitribai Phule was born on 3 January 1831 in Naigaon, Maharashtra, and married Jyotirao Phule in 1840 as a child. He taught her to read.

In 1848 the couple opened a school for girls in Pune. She is often called India's first woman teacher; earlier girls' schools existed, so the "first" claim is contested, and historians also credit Fatima Sheikh as a co-worker.

Accounts say she was harassed with stones and dung on her way to teach.

She and Jyotirao later opened further schools, including for children of lower castes, and in 1863 they founded a home for the prevention of infanticide.

She published a book of poetry, Kavya Phule, in 1854.

credit.work: Savitribai Phule statue, Maharashtra sadan, New Delhi
credit.author: आशीष भटनागर

artists.lifespan: Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake, born between 1831 and 1837, died 1890

works.title: Sitting Bull
works.medium: Sitting Bull by D F Barry ca 1883 Dakota Territory
works.description:
Sitting Bull (Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake, born between 1831 and 1837, died 1890) was a Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man who resisted United States expansion onto Lakota lands and was in the camp at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876. Native police killed him in 1890.

Sitting Bull was born sometime between 1831 and 1837, traditionally on the Grand River in present-day South Dakota (a 2007 family oral tradition places his birth on the Yellowstone River instead), and became a leading Hunkpapa Lakota war leader and holy man.

The Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868) guaranteed the Black Hills to the Lakota. After gold was found there in 1874 the United States sought to take the land, and war followed in 1876.

On 25 and 26 June 1876 Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors destroyed the force of Lt. Col. George Custer at the Little Bighorn. Sitting Bull was in the large camp; accounts describe his role as spiritual leader and organizer rather than field commander.

After the battle he led his followers to Canada in 1877, and he surrendered at Fort Buford in July 1881.

On 15 December 1890, at Standing Rock, Native police sent to arrest him amid tension over the Ghost Dance killed him in a struggle. The Wounded Knee massacre followed on 29 December.

credit.work: Sitting Bull by D F Barry ca 1883 Dakota Territory
credit.author: David F. Barry, Photographer, Bismarck, Dakota Territory

works.title: Christopher Dresser
works.medium: A Victorian 'Komai' solid silver water jug by Christopher Dresser, c.1880
works.description:
Christopher Dresser (1834 to 1904) was a botanist turned designer, now regarded as one of the first modern industrial designers. He worked as an independent consultant for dozens of manufacturers and produced geometric silverware and ceramics that anticipated 20th-century modernism.

Dresser was born in Glasgow in 1834 and trained at the Government School of Design in London. He lectured on botany and in 1859 received a doctorate from the University of Jena for research into plant structure.

He moved into design from about 1858, with ceramic work for firms from the 1860s onwards (sources differ on the start), and published The Art of Decorative Design (1862) and Principles of Decorative Design (1873), arguing that ornament should follow the structural logic of natural forms rather than copy their surface.

In 1876 and 1877 he travelled to Japan, one of the first Western designers to do so, partly on commission from Tiffany & Co. to report on Japanese art and manufacturing.

He designed for Minton, Wedgwood, Coalbrookdale, Hukin & Heath and James Dixon & Sons, and was Art Superintendent of the Linthorpe Art Pottery. He died in 1904.

works.title: Christopher Dresser
works.description:
Christopher Dresser (1834 to 1904) was a botanist turned designer, now regarded as one of the first modern industrial designers. He worked as an independent consultant for dozens of manufacturers and produced geometric silverware and ceramics that anticipated 20th-century modernism.

Dresser was born in Glasgow in 1834 and trained at the Government School of Design in London. He lectured on botany and in 1859 received a doctorate from the University of Jena for research into plant structure.

He moved into design from about 1858, with ceramic work for firms from the 1860s onwards (sources differ on the start), and published The Art of Decorative Design (1862) and Principles of Decorative Design (1873), arguing that ornament should follow the structural logic of natural forms rather than copy their surface.

works.title: William Morris
works.description:
William Morris (1834 to 1896) was an English designer, writer and socialist, the central figure of the Arts and Crafts movement. He rejected cheap mechanised ornament in favour of patterns drawn from nature and made by traditional craft methods.

Morris was born in Walthamstow in 1834 into a family that had grown wealthy through copper mining. At Oxford he met the painter Edward Burne-Jones and, through him, the circle around Dante Gabriel Rossetti.

He built Red House (1859 to 1860) and, unable to find furnishings he considered well made, founded a decorative arts firm in 1861 with Burne-Jones, Rossetti, Philip Webb and others. It was reorganised in 1875 as Morris & Co.

He founded the Socialist League in 1884 and wrote extensively on politics and utopian fiction. In 1891 he founded the Kelmscott Press; its illustrated Chaucer was completed months before his death in 1896.

He designed from real plants, disciplining them into flattened repeating patterns. He revived hand block-printing and indigo-discharge dyeing and letterpress printing from hand-cut type over faster industrial methods.

His principle was "have nothing in your house that you do not know to be useful or believe to be beautiful". His goods were luxuries that generally only the wealthy could afford.

works.title: Cixi
works.description:
The Empress Dowager Cixi (1835 to 1908) was the dominant political figure of late Qing China, ruling as regent for most of the period from 1861 to 1908.

She became regent in 1861 for her young son, the Tongzhi Emperor, and later for the Guangxu Emperor.

Her period includes the Self-Strengthening Movement, an effort to modernize China's defenses and industry.

She supported the Boxers in 1900, and after their defeat she pursued the 'New Policies' reforms.

Historians debate her legacy; older accounts portray her as a reactionary, and recent work stresses her political skill and the limits she faced.

works.title: Liliuokalani
works.description:
Liliuokalani (1838 to 1917) was the last monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaii, reigning from 1891 until she was deposed in January 1893 by a group of residents backed by United States troops.

Liliuokalani was born in Honolulu on 2 September 1838 and died there on 11 November 1917.

She succeeded her brother Kalākaua on 29 January 1891 and was the kingdom's only reigning queen.

In January 1893 she moved to issue a constitution restoring royal powers reduced by the 1887 "Bayonet Constitution."

On 17 January 1893 a Committee of Safety of mostly American and European residents overthrew her while United States Marines were ashore. She yielded to the United States government to avoid bloodshed and asked it to reinstate her.

After a failed royalist uprising she was arrested and signed an abdication in January 1895.

works.title: Claude Monet
works.description:
Claude Monet (14 November 1840 to 5 December 1926) was a French painter, the leader and purest practitioner of Impressionism. His Impression, Sunrise gave the movement its name, and he spent his life painting the changing effects of light.

Monet was born in Paris and grew up in Le Havre, where as a teenager he sold caricatures. Eugène Boudin persuaded him to paint outdoors. In Paris he met Camille Pissarro and befriended Renoir, Sisley and Bazille.

The 1860s and 1870s were years of poverty. During the Franco-Prussian War he took refuge in London, where he saw Turner's paintings and met the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel.

In 1874 he and his friends held an exhibition independent of the official Salon. Critics mocked them, and the name "Impressionist" stuck.

In 1883 his family settled at Giverny in Normandy, where he created a flower garden and a water garden with a Japanese bridge, which became his main subject.

He painted the same subject repeatedly in changing conditions: haystacks, poplars and Rouen Cathedral. Key works include Impression, Sunrise (1872), Stacks of Wheat (1890 to 1891) and the Water Lilies.

works.title: José María Velasco
works.medium: 'Self-portrait' (1877) by José María Velasco - Museo Nacional de Artes - Mexi…
works.description:
José María Velasco (6 July 1840 to 26 August 1912) was the most important Mexican painter of the 19th century, known for panoramic views of the Valley of Mexico. He was also a trained naturalist who illustrated scientific publications on botany, zoology and geology.

Velasco was born in Temascalcingo, in the State of Mexico. His family moved to Mexico City in 1849. In 1858 he entered the Academy of San Carlos, where the Italian painter Eugenio Landesio taught him to observe nature closely and paint outdoors. He also studied botany, zoology, anatomy, physics and mathematics.

In 1877 he succeeded Landesio as professor of landscape painting. Among his students was Diego Rivera.

He worked as a scientific illustrator for the National Museum and on expeditions, and painted archaeological sites such as Teotihuacan.

He won a medal at the Paris Universal Exposition of 1889 and exhibited at the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition. One view of the Valley of Mexico was given to Pope Leo XIII and is now in the Vatican Museums.

He worked from outdoor sketches to large studio compositions. His panoramas set a detailed foreground of cacti and rocks against a luminous distance, and often include railways, bridges and haciendas alongside nature and ruins.

works.title: Yaa Asantewaa
works.description:
Yaa Asantewaa (about 1840 to 1921) was the queen mother of Ejisu in the Asante kingdom, in present-day Ghana, who led an Asante uprising against British rule in 1900. She died in exile in the Seychelles.

Yaa Asantewaa was born about 1840 and was queen mother (ohemaa) of Ejisu, a title held by a woman who advises and helps choose the ruler.

The British exiled the Asante king Prempeh I in 1896. In March 1900 the governor, Frederick Hodgson, demanded the Golden Stool, the Asante symbol of national unity, so that he could sit on it.

According to tradition, she then urged the Asante chiefs at a council to resist and became a leader of the uprising sometimes called the War of the Golden Stool.

Asante forces besieged the British fort at Kumasi for several months in 1900. British reinforcements relieved it, and the fighting ended that year with a British victory.

She was captured and exiled to the Seychelles in 1901, and died there on 17 October 1921.

works.title: Wilfrid Laurier
works.medium: The Honourable Sir Wilfrid Laurier Photo A (3x4 cropped)
works.description:
Wilfrid Laurier (1841 to 1919) was the first French-Canadian Prime Minister of Canada, serving from 1896 to 1911 during a period of rapid western settlement and economic growth.

A lawyer from Quebec, he became Liberal Party leader in 1887 and prime minister in 1896, holding the office for over fifteen years, then the longest unbroken term in Canadian history.

His government promoted immigration and settlement of the Canadian prairies, a policy associated with his minister Clifford Sifton, that brought large numbers of European immigrant farmers to Western Canada.

He worked to balance relations between English- and French-speaking Canada, though his support for Canadian participation in Britain's Boer War strained relations with Quebec nationalists who opposed it.

He lost the 1911 election over a proposed reciprocity (free trade) agreement with the United States, which opponents attacked as a threat to Canada's ties with Britain.

credit.work: The Honourable Sir Wilfrid Laurier Photo A (3x4 cropped)
credit.author: William James Topley

works.title: Mary Cassatt
works.description:
Mary Cassatt (22 May 1844 to 14 June 1926) was an American painter who spent most of her adult life in France and was the only American to exhibit with the French Impressionists. She is celebrated for tender, unsentimental images of women and children.

Cassatt was born in Allegheny City, now part of Pittsburgh, into a wealthy family. Against her father's wishes she studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts from about 1860, then left for Paris in 1866.

Women could not enter the École des Beaux-Arts, so she studied privately and copied Old Masters in the Louvre. Frustrated with the Salon's conservative taste, she accepted Degas's invitation in 1877 to exhibit with the Impressionists, and showed with them in 1879, 1880, 1881 and 1886.

Her parents and sister moved to Paris to live with her, and her family became her favourite models.

In 1890 an exhibition of Japanese prints in Paris inspired a set of colour prints, usually counted as ten, combining drypoint and aquatint. She took from them flat colour, strong outlines and cropped compositions.

In 1893 she painted the mural Modern Woman for the Woman's Building at the Chicago World's Columbian Exposition; it has been lost.

works.title: Menelik II
works.medium: Menelik II in coronation garb, Emperor of Ethiopia
works.description:
Menelik II (1844 to 1913) was emperor of Ethiopia from 1889 and the leader who defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896.

He expanded the empire southward and founded Addis Ababa as the capital.

He imported modern arms and pursued technological modernization.

He won the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896.

His empire's expansion brought conquest of neighboring peoples, and it is debated.

works.title: Ludwig II
works.medium: Albert, Joseph - König Ludwig II. von Bayern (1845-1886) (Zeno Fotografie)
works.description:
Ludwig II (1845 to 1886), sometimes called the "Fairy Tale King," was King of Bavaria from 1864 until his death, remembered for building extravagant romantic castles and for his patronage of the composer Richard Wagner.

He became an early and enthusiastic patron of Richard Wagner, paying off the composer's debts and funding productions, though political opposition to Wagner's influence at court eventually forced the composer to leave Munich.

He commissioned several elaborate castles, most famously Neuschwanstein, begun in 1869 and inspired partly by Wagner's operas; the castles were funded from his personal fortune rather than the Bavarian state treasury but still left him deeply in debt.

Bavaria's defeat alongside Austria in the 1866 Austro-Prussian War, and its incorporation into the German Empire in 1871, steadily reduced his practical political authority even as he retained the throne.

In 1886 a government commission, citing his mounting debts and reclusive behavior, had him declared mentally unfit to rule; he died under unclear circumstances in Lake Starnberg the day after being confined, an event still debated as accident, suicide, or possible foul play.

credit.work: Albert, Joseph - König Ludwig II. von Bayern (1845-1886) (Zeno Fotografie)
credit.author: Josef Albert

works.title: Kate Sheppard
works.description:
Kate Sheppard (1848 to 1934) was an English-born campaigner who led the movement for women's suffrage in New Zealand. The Electoral Act of 1893 made New Zealand the first self-governing country in which women voted in national elections.

Sheppard was born on 10 March 1848 in Liverpool, England, and emigrated to New Zealand, arriving in 1869. She died in Christchurch on 13 July 1934.

From 1887 she was national superintendent for franchise and legislation of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which made votes for women a central aim.

Petitions to Parliament carried about 10,000 signatures in 1891, about 20,000 in 1892 and 31,872 in 1893, the largest petition presented to Parliament until then.

The Governor signed the Electoral Act on 19 September 1893, and women voted for the first time in the election of 28 November 1893.

The Act gave the vote to women of all races, including Māori women in the Māori electorates, but women could not stand for Parliament until 1919.

works.title: Louis Comfort Tiffany
works.description:
Louis Comfort Tiffany (1848 to 1933) was an American designer whose iridescent Favrile glass, stained-glass windows and lamps became the signature look of American Art Nouveau. Recent scholarship credits many of his studio's best-known designs to staff designers, above all Clara Driscoll.

Tiffany was born in New York in 1848, the son of the jeweller Charles Lewis Tiffany. He trained as a painter under George Inness before turning to interior design and decorative arts in the 1870s.

His firm redecorated state rooms in the White House in 1882 for President Chester Arthur; the work was later removed. In 1885 he founded what became Tiffany Studios, and in 1894 he trademarked the name Favrile.

His Byzantine-style chapel for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago won international acclaim. He built Laurelton Hall on Long Island as a showcase of his work.

Favrile glass builds iridescent, metallic colour into molten glass through mineral oxides. "Drapery glass" was manipulated while hot to form folds like fabric.

Financial losses, traced back to the 1920s and continuing into the Depression, forced the studio's closure. He died in New York in 1933.

works.description:
Raja Ravi Varma (29 April 1848 to 2 October 1906) was the most famous Indian painter of the 19th century, from the princely state of Travancore. He brought European academic oil painting to scenes from the Hindu epics, and his mass-produced prints put images of gods and heroines into homes across India.

Ravi Varma was born at Kilimanoor, near Thiruvananthapuram, into an aristocratic family related to the ruling house. By tradition his uncle, the painter Raja Raja Varma, noticed his talent. At 14 he was taken to the palace under Maharaja Ayilyam Thirunal and learned oil painting partly by watching the European portraitist Theodore Jensen.

A portrait won a prize at the 1873 Vienna exhibition, and his work was shown at the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition, where it won three gold medals. He painted a series of Puranic subjects for Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda in 1888 to 1890.

In 1894 he set up a lithographic press at Ghatkopar in Bombay, and moved it in 1899 to Malavli near Lonavala, producing colour prints (oleographs) of deities and heroines that sold in huge numbers. Critics accused him of vulgarising sacred subjects.

In 1904 the British Viceroy awarded him the Kaisar-i-Hind Gold Medal. He died at Attingal.

He combined Victorian academic realism with Indian subjects and costumes. His heroines were based on real women and staged at dramatic moments.

works.title: Antoni Gaudí
works.description:
Antoni Gaudí (25 June 1852 to 10 June 1926) was the leading architect of Catalan Modernisme, the regional cousin of Art Nouveau. Almost all his mature work stands in Barcelona, and it culminates in the still-unfinished Sagrada Família.

Gaudí was born in Reus or possibly the neighbouring Riudoms, Catalonia (sources differ, and from 1915 he himself said Riudoms), the youngest son of a coppersmith. He credited his father's workshop with teaching him to see three-dimensional space. He graduated from the Barcelona School of Architecture in 1878.

The industrialist Eusebi Güell noticed a display case he designed for a glove-maker at the Paris World's Fair and became his patron for the rest of his career.

He never married, grew increasingly devout, and by his sixties lived an almost monastic life devoted to the Sagrada Família.

On 7 June 1926 he was struck by a tram while walking to church in shabby clothes. Mistaken for a beggar, he received delayed care and died on 10 June. He was buried in the crypt of his unfinished basilica.

He modelled forms on nature and hung scale models of chains and sandbags, photographed upside down, to find the ideal shape for a compression-only arch. He revived trencadís, mosaic of broken tile, as a cheap weatherproof skin.

works.title: Emperor Meiji
works.description:
Emperor Meiji (1852 to 1912) was the Emperor of Japan from 1867, in whose name the Meiji Restoration transformed Japan into a modern industrial state.

He came to the throne in 1867 at the age of about fourteen.

The Charter Oath (1868) was issued in his name, promising reform.

His reign saw a new constitution (1889), industrialization, and Japan's rise as a regional power.

He died in 1912.

works.title: José Martí
works.medium: José Martí retrato hecho en México 1875
works.description:
José Martí (1853 to 1895) was a Cuban poet, journalist and organizer who founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party in 1892 and helped launch the 1895 war of independence against Spain. He was killed in one of its first battles.

Martí was born in Havana on 28 January 1853. Arrested at 16 over a letter criticizing a schoolmate who joined the Spanish army, he was sentenced to six years' hard labor and deported to Spain in 1871. He later lived in Mexico, Guatemala, Venezuela and, from 1880, mainly New York.

He published Ismaelillo (1882), Versos sencillos (1891) and the essay "Nuestra América" (1891), which argued that Latin American countries should govern from knowledge of their own peoples.

In 1892 he founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party and its newspaper Patria, arguing for a republic open to all races and against United States expansion into Cuba.

He landed in eastern Cuba on 11 April 1895 and was killed at Dos Ríos on 19 May in his first engagement. Cuba became formally independent in 1902, under limits set by the United States.

Both the Cuban government and Cuban exile groups have since claimed him as a symbol.

credit.work: José Martí retrato hecho en México 1875
credit.author: Cuba. Secretaría de Instrucción Pública y Bellas Artes.

works.title: Vincent van Gogh
works.medium: Vincent van Gogh - Self-Portrait - Google Art Project (454045)
works.description:
Vincent van Gogh (30 March 1853 to 29 July 1890) was a Dutch painter who worked in France. He painted for only about ten years, produced around 2,100 works, and sold almost nothing, yet his vivid colour and expressive brushwork made him the most famous artist of modern times.

Van Gogh was born in Zundert in the southern Netherlands, the son of a Protestant minister. At 16 he joined the art dealers Goupil & Cie and was dismissed in 1876. He then tried teaching and preaching among coal miners in the Borinage. In 1880 he decided to become an artist.

His younger brother Theo, an art dealer, supported him for the rest of his life. His letters, mainly to Theo, are among the most moving documents of any artist's life.

In 1886 he moved to Paris, where he met Pissarro, Toulouse-Lautrec, Émile Bernard and Gauguin and discovered Impressionist colour and Japanese prints. He painted copies of two Hiroshige prints.

In 1888 he moved to Arles. Gauguin joined him in October, and the partnership collapsed in December after Van Gogh cut off part of his own ear. He entered the asylum at Saint-Rémy in May 1889, where he painted The Starry Night.

In May 1890 he moved to Auvers-sur-Oise and painted about one canvas a day. He shot himself on 27 July 1890 and died two days later, aged 37.

works.title: Teddy Roosevelt
works.medium: Theodore Roosevelt by the Pach Bros (4x5 cropped) (2)
works.description:
Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt (1858 to 1919) was the 26th President of the United States, serving from 1901 to 1909, known for trust-busting antitrust policy, an assertive foreign policy, and a major expansion of federal land conservation.

He became president in 1901 after the assassination of William McKinley, at 42 the youngest person to hold the office, and was elected in his own right in 1904.

He pursued antitrust action against major corporate combinations, including a successful suit against the Northern Securities Company railroad trust in 1904, and mediated the 1902 coal strike partly by threatening to send in federal troops to run the mines.

He established the United States Forest Service and used his executive authority to create national forests, wildlife refuges, and national monuments, protecting roughly 230 million acres of land during his presidency.

After leaving office he attempted a comeback in the 1912 election on a progressive "Bull Moose" third-party ticket, splitting the Republican vote and helping elect Woodrow Wilson instead.

credit.work: Theodore Roosevelt by the Pach Bros (4x5 cropped) (2)
credit.author: Adam Cuerden

works.title: Henry Ossawa Tanner
works.description:
Henry Ossawa Tanner (21 June 1859 to 25 May 1937) was an American painter, the first African American artist to win international fame. Frustrated by racism at home, he settled in Paris in 1891 and built his career there, painting dignified genre scenes and luminous biblical subjects.

Tanner was born in Pittsburgh, the eldest of nine children. His father, Benjamin Tucker Tanner, became a bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and his mother, Sarah, had escaped slavery via the Underground Railroad. At 13 he decided to become an artist.

In 1879 he enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and studied with Thomas Eakins. He was the only Black student and faced harassment. He left for Europe in 1891 and studied at the Académie Julian in Paris.

On a return visit in 1893 he painted The Banjo Lesson, and he painted The Thankful Poor in 1894, both genre scenes of Black American life that challenged racist stereotypes.

Back in France he turned to biblical subjects. The Resurrection of Lazarus won a medal at the 1897 Salon, and the French government bought it. His patron Rodman Wanamaker paid for trips to Egypt and Palestine.

He married the singer Jessie Olsson in 1899. He was made a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur in 1923 and died in Paris.

works.title: Alphonse Mucha
works.description:
Alphonse Mucha (1860 to 1939) was a Moravian-born designer whose decorative posters for Sarah Bernhardt and commercial clients defined the visual style of Art Nouveau. He resisted that label and saw his true work in a cycle of paintings on the history of the Slavic peoples.

Mucha was born in Ivančice in Moravia, then part of the Austrian Empire, and worked as a theatrical scene painter before moving to Paris in 1887.

In December 1894 a Paris printing house needed a poster for Sarah Bernhardt's play Gismonda at short notice over the holidays and turned to Mucha as the only designer available. Its success led Bernhardt to sign him to a six-year contract for posters, sets and costumes.

In 1902 he published Documents décoratifs, a pattern book of his ornamental style for other designers and craftsmen.

From about 1910 he devoted much of his career to The Slav Epic, a cycle of twenty monumental canvases on Slavic history, which he donated to the city of Prague. It was put on display at the National Gallery Prague's Trade Fair Palace in 2012.

His formula was elongated women within ornamental frames, reproduced in muted colour lithography on theatre posters, cigarette papers, bicycles and calendars, reaching shops, cafés and middle-class homes across Europe.

works.title: Georges Méliès
works.description:
Georges Méliès (1861 to 1938) was a Paris stage magician who became a filmmaker and invented cinema's first special effects. Over roughly 500 films in under twenty years, including A Trip to the Moon (1902), he turned the new camera from a device for recording reality into a machine for staging the impossible.

Méliès was born in Paris to a prosperous shoe-manufacturing family and wanted to study painting, but his father would not support him as an artist and he supervised machinery at the family factory. In about 1888 he bought the Théâtre Robert-Houdin, a famous conjuring theatre.

After attending the Lumière brothers' first public film screening in December 1895, he tried to buy a camera from them and was refused. He acquired one from a British inventor and built a studio at Montreuil with a glass-walled stage.

About 1896 he discovered, by accident when his camera jammed mid-shot, that stopping and restarting filming could make objects vanish or transform. This became the "stop trick" behind his trick films.

His techniques included stop-motion substitution, multiple exposure, dissolves, painted sets built to force perspective, and hand-tinted colour done frame by frame by a team of women colourists.

American piracy of his films, the rise of narrative studio filmmaking and the disruption of the First World War ruined his business. He was reduced to running a toy stall in a Paris train station.

works.title: José Rizal
works.description:
José Rizal (1861 to 1896) was a Filipino physician, writer and reformer whose novels criticized Spanish colonial rule. Spanish authorities executed him in Manila on 30 December 1896, and he is regarded as a national hero of the Philippines.

Rizal was born on 19 June 1861 in Calamba, in the Philippines. He studied in Manila, Madrid, Paris and Heidelberg and became an eye doctor.

He wrote the novels Noli Me Tángere (1887) and El Filibusterismo (1891), which portrayed abuses by Spanish friars and officials; the colonial authorities banned them.

In 1892 he founded La Liga Filipina, a reform society, and was exiled to Dapitan on Mindanao, where he practiced medicine and taught until 1896.

The Philippine Revolution began in August 1896. Rizal, who had volunteered as a doctor in Cuba, was arrested on his way there, brought back to Manila and convicted of rebellion. He had said he opposed an armed uprising at that time.

He was shot by firing squad on 30 December 1896, aged 35. Before his death he wrote a poem now known as "Mi último adiós."

works.description:
Gustav Klimt (14 July 1862 to 6 February 1918) was an Austrian painter and the leader of the Vienna Secession. His golden, patterned paintings of women and love, above all The Kiss, are icons of turn-of-the-century Vienna.

Klimt was born at Baumgarten near Vienna, the second of seven children of a gold engraver. He won a scholarship to the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts in 1876 and, with his brother Ernst and Franz Matsch, painted murals and ceilings for the Burgtheater and the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

In 1897 he became the first president of the Vienna Secession, a group breaking from the official academy with the motto "To every age its art, to art its freedom".

His ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna, showing Philosophy, Medicine and Jurisprudence, caused a scandal over nudity and pessimism. He withdrew from the commission, and the paintings were destroyed in a fire in 1945.

He never married, had a lifelong companionship with the designer Emilie Flöge and fathered several children with models. He supported younger artists such as Egon Schiele and Oskar Kokoschka. He died in Vienna after a stroke.

In his "golden period" (about 1899 to 1910) he applied real gold and silver leaf, drawing on Byzantine mosaics he saw in Ravenna in 1903, and on Japanese and Egyptian art. Key works include The Kiss (1907 to 1908) and the Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907).

works.title: Hilma af Klint
works.medium: Hilma af Klint, portrait photograph published in 1901
works.description:
Hilma af Klint (26 October 1862 to 21 October 1944) was a Swedish painter who, from 1906, created hundreds of abstract paintings guided by her spiritual beliefs, several years before Kandinsky, Mondrian and Malevich. She kept them largely hidden, and they reached an international audience only from the 1980s.

Af Klint was born at Karlberg Palace in Solna, near Stockholm. She studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Stockholm from 1882 to 1887 and made a living painting landscapes, portraits and botanical illustrations.

Her spiritual investigations, which sources date from 1879, developed around the time of the death of her younger sister Hermina in 1880 and drew her toward spiritualism and Theosophy. With four other women, who began as members of the Edelweiss Society, she made up "The Five", which held séances and experimented with automatic drawing, which the sources date to 1896.

In 1906, believing she had received a commission from a spiritual guide, she began the Paintings for the Temple, a cycle of nearly 200 works completed in 1915. She considered herself a medium through whom the works were created.

In 1908 she showed her work to Rudolf Steiner. His cool response contributed to a four-year break in the series. She later spent long periods at the Goetheanum, the Anthroposophical Society's headquarters, between 1921 and 1930, and filled more than 125 notebooks, with sources giving figures from 125 to more than 150.

She believed the world was not ready for the paintings and directed that they not be exhibited until 20 years after her death. She died after a traffic accident, leaving more than 1,200 paintings and drawings to her nephew.

works.title: Lumière Brothers
works.description:
Auguste Lumière (1862 to 1954) and Louis Lumière (1864 to 1948) were French manufacturers of photographic plates who patented the Cinématographe in 1895 and staged the first paying public screening of projected motion pictures. The dates here run from Auguste's birth to his death.

The brothers were born in Besançon and grew up in Lyon, where their father Antoine ran a portrait studio and later a factory making dry photographic plates.

After their father saw a demonstration of Edison's single-viewer Kinetoscope in 1894, they set out to build a device that could project moving images to a seated audience. Louis is generally credited with the key mechanical insight, adapting the sewing machine's intermittent claw movement to advance the film.

They patented the Cinématographe in February 1895, one device that could shoot, print and project. Their first paying public screening was on 28 December 1895 in the Salon Indien of the Grand Café in Paris, traditionally described as a basement on the Boulevard des Capucines: ten short films for roughly thirty-five to forty people, though accounts differ.

Their "actuality" films were usually a single static, unedited shot of under a minute. L'Arroseur arrosé is a rare staged gag, effectively cinema's first fiction film. Key works include Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory (1895) and The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat (1896).

They sent camera operators around the world, spreading projected cinema to India, Japan, Australia and the Americas within a year or two.

works.title: Edvard Munch
works.description:
Edvard Munch (12 December 1863 to 23 January 1944) was a Norwegian painter and printmaker who turned illness, grief, love and fear into images of inner states. The Scream became an emblem of the modern psyche, and he is a founding figure of Expressionism.

Munch was born in Løten, Norway, and grew up in Kristiania (now Oslo). His mother died of tuberculosis when he was five and his sister Sophie of the same disease when he was 13. Another sister was later hospitalised for mental illness.

In the 1890s he lived mostly in Berlin and Paris and developed the Frieze of Life cycle. His 1892 exhibition in Berlin was closed after a week amid scandal, which made him famous in Germany.

He suffered a breakdown in 1908 and was treated in Copenhagen. From 1916 he lived at his estate, Ekely, outside Oslo. In 1937 the Nazis labelled his work "degenerate" and removed it from German museums.

He simplified forms into flowing outlines and flat expressive colour, influenced by Van Gogh, Gauguin and Symbolism. His woodcuts and lithographs are as important as his paintings.

Key works include The Sick Child (1885 to 1886), The Scream (1893), Madonna (1894) and The Dance of Life (1899 to 1900).

works.title: Sun Yat-sen
works.description:
Sun Yat-sen (1866 to 1925) was a Chinese revolutionary and physician who worked for decades to overthrow the Qing dynasty and became the first provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912. Both mainland China and Taiwan honor him as a founder.

Sun Yat-sen was born on 12 November 1866 in Cuiheng, Guangdong, and died on 12 March 1925 in Beijing. He was educated in Hawaii and trained as a doctor in Hong Kong, graduating in 1892.

He founded the Revive China Society in 1894, after an earlier reform petition was rejected, and organized several failed uprisings against the Qing from 1895 onward.

In Tokyo in 1905 he founded the Tongmenghui, which grew to about a thousand members, and set out his Three Principles of the People: nationalism, democracy and people's livelihood.

The Wuchang uprising of 10 October 1911, which he did not lead in person, began the revolution that ended the Qing dynasty. He returned from abroad and served as provisional president from 1 January 1912, resigning that March to Yuan Shikai.

He rebuilt his Kuomintang party in 1919, and in 1923 allied it with the Soviet Union and the small Chinese Communist Party.

works.title: Wassily Kandinsky
works.medium: Kandinsky - Vassily Kandinsky by Adolf Elnain Photo credits - Georges Meguerd…
works.description:
Wassily Kandinsky (16 December 1866 to 13 December 1944) was a Russian painter and theorist, one of the first to create purely abstract works in Europe. He believed colours and forms, freed from depicting objects, could move the viewer as directly as music.

Kandinsky was born in Moscow and grew up in Odessa. He studied law and economics and began an academic career. In 1896, having seen one of Monet's Haystacks and heard Wagner's Lohengrin, he gave up law and moved to Munich to study painting.

In 1911 he and Franz Marc founded Der Blaue Reiter (The Blue Rider) and he published On the Spiritual in Art. About then he painted his first fully abstract works.

The First World War forced him back to Russia, where he took part in Soviet cultural institutions after the 1917 Revolution. He returned to Germany in 1920 or 1921 (sources differ) and taught at the Bauhaus from 1922 to 1933.

When the Nazis closed the Bauhaus he moved to Neuilly-sur-Seine near Paris, becoming a French citizen in 1939, and died there.

He sorted his works into Impressions, Improvisations and Compositions, and made only ten Compositions over 30 years. He probably experienced synaesthesia and assigned musical qualities to colours: yellow like a trumpet, blue like a deep cello.

works.title: Frank Lloyd Wright
works.description:
Frank Lloyd Wright (1867 to 1959) was the most influential American architect of the 20th century. Over seven decades he argued for "organic architecture", buildings designed from the inside out around their site, materials and users.

Wright was born in Richland Center, Wisconsin, studied engineering briefly at the University of Wisconsin and moved to Chicago, where he worked under Louis Sullivan, whom he later called his "Lieber Meister".

He set up his own practice in Oak Park in the 1890s and developed the low, wide-eaved Prairie house style. His personal life was turbulent: an affair, the killing of seven people at his Wisconsin home Taliesin in 1914, and bankruptcy during the Depression.

In his late sixties he designed Fallingwater and the Johnson Wax headquarters (both 1936 to 1939), and finally the Guggenheim Museum (design and construction from 1943 to 1959). He died in 1959 aged 91.

He designed around open, flowing interior space, with art-glass bands and deep cantilevered overhangs, and used concrete, steel and glass without disguising them as historical stonework. He designed most of the furniture, textiles and stained glass in his buildings himself.

He designed more than a thousand structures, roughly half built. Fallingwater and several others are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

works.title: Marie Curie
works.description:
Marie Curie (1867 to 1934) was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered research on radioactivity and is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel.

She won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering polonium and radium.

She developed mobile X-ray units for use in World War I hospitals.

She died of aplastic anemia, likely caused by long exposure to radiation.

works.title: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
works.description:
Charles Rennie Mackintosh (1868 to 1928) was a Glasgow architect-designer who led the "Glasgow Style" of Art Nouveau, treating buildings, furniture and interiors as one unified art. His Glasgow School of Art and total interior schemes made him a major influence on European design, though home recognition came only after his death.

Born in Glasgow in 1868, Mackintosh trained as an architect while attending evening classes at the Glasgow School of Art, where he met his future wife, artist Margaret Macdonald.

With Macdonald, her sister Frances and Herbert MacNair, he formed "The Four," a symbolist group whose style became the Glasgow Style.

At Honeyman and Keppie he won an anonymous 1896 competition for his own art school's new building; its 1909 completion made his reputation.

He then designed houses, tearooms and a school around Glasgow, including Hill House (1902-1904), the Willow Tearooms (1903) and Scotland Street School (1903-1906), with Macdonald designing the furnishings throughout.

His towering ladder-back chairs, shaped as much to define a room as to be sat in, became his best-known design.

works.title: Mahatma Gandhi
works.description:
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869 to 1948) was an Indian lawyer and political leader who led the movement for Indian independence using nonviolent resistance.

He developed satyagraha (insistence on truth), first in South Africa, then in India.

The Salt March of 1930 was a major act of civil disobedience.

India became independent in 1947 and was partitioned; he opposed partition.

He was assassinated in January 1948.

works.title: Alice Guy-Blaché
works.description:
Alice Guy-Blaché (1873–1968) was a French filmmaker who began directing at the Gaumont Film Company in Paris in 1896 and later became the first woman to found and run her own film studio. She is credited as one of cinema's earliest narrative directors, though her work was erased from film history for most of the twentieth century.

Born in Saint-Mandé, France, in 1873, she was hired as a secretary in 1894 at a camera and photography supply company, which Léon Gaumont and partners took over in 1895 as it moved into motion pictures.

After seeing an early demonstration film, she won permission to direct in her spare time; the result, traditionally given as La Fée aux choux (1896), is often called cinema's first narrative film, though its title is uncertain and that 1896 film appears to be lost, with the surviving 1900 and 1902 versions being different films.

She rose to head of production at Gaumont, experimenting with hand-tinted colour and an early sound process, Phonoscènes, and in 1906 satirized gender roles in the reversal comedy Les Résultats du féminisme.

In 1907 she married cameraman Herbert Blaché, moved to the United States, and in 1910 co-founded the Solax Company in Flushing, New York, where she was artistic director, with a new plant at Fort Lee, New Jersey following in 1912.

At Solax she directed social dramas like Making an American Citizen and Falling Leaves (1912), tackling immigration and domestic abuse more directly than most peers.

She rose to head of production at Gaumont, experimenting with hand-tinted colour and an early sound process, Phonoscènes, and in 1906 satirized gender roles in the reversal comedy Les Résultats du féminisme.

In 1907 she married cameraman Herbert Blaché, moved to the United States, and in 1910 co-founded the Solax Company in Flushing, New York, where she was artistic director, with a new plant at Fort Lee, New Jersey following in 1912.

At Solax she directed social dramas like Making an American Citizen and Falling Leaves (1912), tackling immigration and domestic abuse more directly than most peers.

works.title: Albert Einstein
works.description:
Albert Einstein (1879 to 1955) was a German-born physicist who developed the theories of special and general relativity and made key contributions to quantum theory.

In 1905 he published papers on special relativity, the photoelectric effect, and Brownian motion.

General relativity (1915) describes gravity as the curvature of space and time.

He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for the photoelectric effect.

In 1939 he signed a letter to President Roosevelt about the possibility of atomic weapons.

works.title: Knud Rasmussen
works.medium: Den danske polarforsker Knud Rasmussen modtager Charley P. Darby's guldmedalj…
works.description:
Knud Rasmussen (1879 to 1933) was a Danish-Greenlandic explorer and ethnographer who recorded Inuit oral traditions and led the Fifth Thule Expedition (1921 to 1924), a dog-sled journey from Greenland across Arctic Canada to Alaska.

Knud Rasmussen was born on 7 June 1879 in Jakobshavn (Ilulissat), Greenland, to a Danish missionary father and a mother of part Greenlandic Inuit descent, and grew up speaking Greenlandic.

In 1910 he and Peter Freuchen founded the Thule Trading Station at Cape York in northwest Greenland, which helped fund his expeditions.

On the Fifth Thule Expedition he traveled with Greenlandic Inuit companions across northern Canada to Alaska. The expedition's archaeologist, Therkel Mathiassen, excavated sites that led to the identification of the Thule culture.

He collected songs, stories and accounts of belief from the Iglulik and other Inuit groups, and wrote Across Arctic America (1927).

He fell ill on the Seventh Thule Expedition and died in Copenhagen on 21 December 1933.

works.title: John Curtin
works.description:
John Curtin (1885 to 1945) was Prime Minister of Australia from 1941 to 1945, leading the country through the Pacific war against Japan during the Second World War.

A former journalist and trade unionist who had opposed conscription during the First World War, he became Labor Party leader in 1935 and prime minister in October 1941.

After Japan entered the war in December 1941 and bombed Darwin in February 1942, he redirected Australian forces from the European theatre and, over British objections, recalled Australian troops from the Middle East to defend against Japanese advance.

He committed Australia more closely to the United States for wartime defense, stating in December 1941 that Australia looked to America "free of any pangs" about its traditional ties to Britain.

He introduced wartime economic controls and expanded the Australian government's role in social welfare, but died in office in July 1945, weeks before Japan's surrender, worn down by the strain of the war years.

works.title: Buster Keaton
works.description:
Buster Keaton (1895 to 1966) was an American silent-film comedian, writer and director known as the deadpan "Great Stone Face," who built his comedy on engineered physical stunts he performed himself. Ranked with Charlie Chaplin among silent comedy's defining stars, he made The General (1926), now considered among the greatest films ever made.

Born in 1895 into a vaudeville family, Keaton performed from age three in the act The Three Keatons, taking falls that built his later physical control.

He entered film in 1917 under Roscoe "Fatty" Arbuckle, and by 1920 was writing, directing and starring in his own comedies, moving into features with Our Hospitality (1923).

Sherlock Jr. (1924) placed him inside a shifting film-dream using in-camera measurement rather than editing tricks, still studied for its daring.

The Navigator (1924), about passengers adrift on an ocean liner, was his biggest commercial success of the decade.

The General (1926), built around full-scale trains and a locomotive plunged off a burning bridge, flopped on release but is now ranked among cinema's greatest films.

works.title: Sergei Eisenstein
works.description:
Sergei Eisenstein (1898 to 1948) was a Soviet film director and theorist, born in Riga, who argued that meaning came from the collision between shots rather than any single image. His Odessa Steps massacre sequence in Battleship Potemkin (1925) remains one of cinema's most studied passages.

Eisenstein was born in Riga in 1898, son of an architect and civil engineer, and trained in engineering and architecture before turning to the arts.

The Russian Revolution pushed him into theatre; he joined Meyerhold's Proletkult Theatre before moving into film in the early 1920s.

His second feature, Battleship Potemkin (1925), made for the twentieth anniversary of the 1905 Revolution, brought him international fame.

In Strike (1925) he pioneered "intellectual montage," cutting colliding images together and favoring crowds and non-professional "types" over trained stars.

Invited to Hollywood then Mexico in the early 1930s, both projects went unfinished, and his 1937 Soviet film Bezhin Meadow was suppressed and reportedly destroyed.

works.title: Frida Kahlo
works.description:
Frida Kahlo (1907 to 1954) was a Mexican painter, best known for small, vivid self-portraits made in Mexico City. She worked through years of pain after a bus accident in 1925 and became a global cultural icon after her death.

Kahlo was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacán, now part of Mexico City. She often gave 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution began, as her birth year.

A bus accident on 17 September 1925 broke her spine, pelvis and right leg and ended her plan to study medicine. She began painting during her recovery.

She married the muralist Diego Rivera in 1929, divorced him in 1939 and remarried him in 1940.

Estimates of her output run from fewer than 150 to about 200 paintings, most of them self-portraits, including The Two Fridas (1939) and The Broken Column (1944).

Her first solo show was at the Julien Levy Gallery in New York in 1938. In 1939 the Louvre bought her painting The Frame, the first work by a Mexican artist in its collection.

works.title: Alan Turing
works.description:
Alan Turing (1912 to 1954) was a British mathematician who formalized the concept of computation, helped break German ciphers in World War II, and proposed a test for machine intelligence.

In 1936 he described the abstract 'Turing machine', a foundation of computer science.

At Bletchley Park he worked on breaking the Enigma cipher.

In 1950 he published a paper proposing what became known as the Turing test.

He was prosecuted in 1952 for homosexuality, then a crime in Britain, and received a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.

works.title: Amrita Sher-Gil
works.description:
Amrita Sher-Gil (1913 to 1941) was a Hungarian-Indian painter, born in Budapest to a Sikh father and a Hungarian-Jewish mother, who trained in Paris before returning to India to paint its people, especially its women. Often called India's first great modern woman artist, she fused European Post-Impressionist technique with Ajanta murals and Mughal-Rajput miniature painting across barely a decade of work.

Born in Budapest on 30 January 1913 to a Sikh father and a Hungarian-Jewish mother, she moved to India in 1921 and began painting as a child in Shimla.

She studied art in Paris from about 1929 (sources date her attendance at Parisian art schools from 1930), and in 1933 became the youngest associate, and the only Asian, elected to the Grand Salon.

Returning to India in 1934, a 1937 journey through South India and the Ajanta murals reshaped her style into simplified, monumental figures in flat colour.

Three Girls (1935) won the Bombay Art Society's gold medal in 1937, the year she also painted Bride's Toilet and Brahmacharis; later works such as Village Scene (1938) and Haldi Grinders (1940) drew on Indian miniature painting to depict rural women's lives.

She married her Hungarian cousin, Victor Egan, in 1938; the couple later settled at Saraya in Uttar Pradesh before moving to Lahore in 1941.

works.title: Muhammad Ali of Egypt
works.medium: ModernEgypt, Muhammad Ali by Auguste Couder, BAP 17996
works.description:
Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer of Albanian family, became governor of Egypt in 1805, destroyed the old Mamluk elite, built a conscript army and state-run economy, and founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt until 1952.

Muhammad Ali was born in Kavala, in what is now Greece, to an Albanian family from the Korçë region. His father was a tobacco merchant and an Ottoman military commander.

He rose to power after the French withdrawal from Egypt in 1801. In 1805 prominent Egyptians, including the religious scholars, demanded his appointment as governor (wali), and the Ottomans accepted.

In 1811 he invited the leading Mamluks to a celebration at the Cairo Citadel, where his forces ambushed and killed them. More Mamluks were then hunted down in Cairo and elsewhere, for a total of perhaps 3,000.

He introduced long-staple cotton, built an army of conscripts trained by European officers, and set up a state-run industrial economy.

He founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt until 1952.

works.title: Toussaint Louverture
works.description:
Toussaint Louverture was a formerly enslaved man who became the principal military and political leader of the Haitian Revolution, and died in a French prison in 1803.

He was born into slavery on Saint-Domingue around 1743 (20 May 1743 in one account) and was freed in 1776 or 1777, depending on the source, before the revolution began in 1791.

He began as a lieutenant in the 1791 uprising and at first allied with the Spanish of neighboring Santo Domingo. In 1794 he switched to the French Republic, which had abolished slavery, and in 1798 he negotiated the withdrawal of British forces under a treaty with General Thomas Maitland.

On 7 July 1801 he promulgated a constitution asserting his authority over the whole island of Hispaniola, which made him governor-general for life.

Napoleon sent an expedition in 1802; Toussaint was arrested by deception and deported to France, where he died at Fort de Joux in April 1803.

Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed Haiti's independence on 1 January 1804.

works.title: Eleanor Roosevelt
works.medium: Eleanor Roosevelt at the United Nations, circa 1946-1947 (3x4 cropped)
works.description:
Eleanor Roosevelt (1884 to 1962) was First Lady of the United States from 1933 to 1945 and afterward a diplomat who chaired the United Nations commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

She was born on 11 October 1884 in New York City and married Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1905.

As First Lady she redefined the role, holding her own press conferences, writing a daily newspaper column, and speaking for civil rights and the poor, sometimes publicly differing with her husband's policies.

After his death in 1945, President Truman appointed her a delegate to the new United Nations in December 1945.

She chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights, which drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the General Assembly on 10 December 1948. She called this her greatest achievement.

She later chaired a presidential commission on the status of women under President Kennedy.

works.title: Ho Chi Minh
works.description:
Ho Chi Minh (1890 to 1969) was a Vietnamese revolutionary who led the movement against French rule, headed the provisional government in 1945, and became the first president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in 1946, an office he held until his death during the Vietnam War.

He was born on 19 May 1890 in Nghệ An province, French-ruled Vietnam, as Nguyễn Sinh Cung, and later used many names, including Nguyễn Ái Quốc and, from about 1943, Hồ Chí Minh.

He left Vietnam in 1911 and lived in Britain, France, the Soviet Union and China. In early 1930, in Hong Kong, he chaired the merger of Vietnamese communist groups into one party.

He returned to Vietnam in 1941 to lead the Việt Minh independence front, and on 2 September 1945 in Hanoi read the declaration of independence, opening by quoting the American and French declarations of rights.

The First Indochina War ended with the Việt Minh victory at Điện Biên Phủ in 1954. Vietnam was partitioned at the 17th parallel, and the 1956 reunification elections were never held.

In the North's 1953 to 1956 land reform, many people were wrongly executed, with estimates from about a thousand to tens of thousands; he apologized in 1956 for serious errors.

works.title: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti
works.description:
Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (1900 to 1978) was a Nigerian teacher and campaigner who led the Abeokuta Women's Union in protests against a tax on women and against the local ruler, the Alake of Egbaland, in the 1940s.

Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti was born on 25 October 1900 in Abeokuta, in southwestern Nigeria. She studied there and in Cheshire, England, from 1919 to 1922.

In 1925 she married the Reverend Israel Oludotun Ransome-Kuti. Their children included the musician Fela Kuti and the physicians Beko and Olikoye Ransome-Kuti.

She founded the Abeokuta Ladies' Club in 1932. It became the Abeokuta Women's Union about 1946 and is reported to have had about 20,000 members.

In the late 1940s the union protested a tax on women and the rule of the Alake, Ademola II, who was forced to leave the throne for a time in 1949.

She helped found the Federation of Nigerian Women's Societies in 1953 and received the Lenin Peace Prize in 1970.

works.title: Sukarno
works.description:
Sukarno (1901 to 1970) was the leader of Indonesia's independence movement and its first president. He proclaimed independence in 1945, ruled until 1967, and was removed from power after the killings of 1965 and 1966.

Sukarno was born on 6 June 1901 in Surabaya, in the Dutch East Indies, and died on 21 June 1970 in Jakarta, under house arrest.

He founded the Indonesian National Party in 1927. The Dutch arrested him in 1929 and released him in 1931, then exiled him to Flores in 1934 and to Sumatra in 1938.

He cooperated with the Japanese occupation from 1942 to 1945, which forced millions into labor and whose food requisitions contributed to a famine that killed over a million people in Java in 1944 and 1945.

On 1 June 1945 he presented Pancasila, five founding principles for the state, and on 17 August 1945 he proclaimed independence, becoming president the next day.

He hosted the Bandung Conference of Asian and African states in 1955 and introduced "Guided Democracy" in 1959, ending parliamentary rule.

works.title: Rachel Carson
works.description:
Rachel Carson (1907 to 1964) was an American marine biologist and writer whose book 'Silent Spring' (1962) helped launch the modern environmental movement.

Silent Spring documented the harm that pesticides such as DDT caused to birds and ecosystems.

The book prompted government action; the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency was created in 1970 and DDT was banned for most uses in the U.S. in 1972.

Chemical industry groups attacked her work.

She died of breast cancer in 1964.

works.title: Indira Gandhi
works.description:
Indira Gandhi (1917 to 1984) was prime minister of India for most of 1966 to 1984. She led India through the 1971 war that created Bangladesh, imposed emergency rule from 1975 to 1977, and was assassinated by her own bodyguards after ordering an army raid on Sikhism's holiest shrine.

She was born on 19 November 1917 in Allahabad, daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, and became prime minister herself in 1966.

In 1971 India backed the independence of East Pakistan, which became Bangladesh, after a short war with Pakistan.

On 25 June 1975 she had a state of emergency declared, suspending civil liberties, censoring the press and jailing opponents, until elections in 1977 that she lost.

She returned to power in 1980. Government policy also pushed the Green Revolution's higher-yield crops during her years in office.

In June 1984 she ordered Operation Blue Star, a military assault on the Golden Temple in Amritsar to remove armed Sikh militants, which damaged the shrine and angered many Sikhs.

works.title: Nelson Mandela
works.description:
Nelson Mandela (1918 to 2013) was a South African anti-apartheid leader who was imprisoned for 27 years and became the country's first democratically elected president in 1994.

He co-founded the African National Congress Youth League and helped lead the resistance to apartheid.

He was imprisoned from 1962 to 1990.

After release, he negotiated the end of apartheid.

He served as president from 1994 to 1999.

works.title: Rosalind Franklin
works.description:
Rosalind Franklin (1920 to 1958) was a British chemist whose X-ray images of DNA were crucial to the discovery of its double-helix structure.

'Photo 51', an X-ray image of DNA, was taken in 1952 by Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling.

Her data were shown to James Watson without her knowledge and helped him and Francis Crick propose the structure in 1953.

She died of ovarian cancer at 37, four years before Watson, Crick, and Maurice Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize.

She also did important work on coal and on viruses.

works.title: Wangari Maathai
works.description:
Wangari Maathai (1940 to 2011) was a Kenyan environmental and political activist who founded the Green Belt Movement, which organized women to plant trees, and in 2004 became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

Maathai was born on 1 April 1940 in Ihithe, near Nyeri, Kenya. She studied biology in the United States and at the University of Nairobi, where she received a doctorate in 1971; she is recorded as the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn one.

In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement, which organized women to plant tree seedlings against deforestation, soil loss and fuelwood shortage.

Her campaigns against building projects on public land in Nairobi and against forest clearing brought clashes with the government of President Daniel arap Moi; she was arrested and at times injured.

She was elected to parliament in 2002 and served as an assistant minister for the environment from 2003.

She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004. In the same year a Kenyan newspaper reported that she had said HIV was deliberately created by scientists; she denied saying it and stated that she did not hold that belief.

works.title: Chico Mendes
works.description:
Chico Mendes (Francisco Alves Mendes Filho, 1944 to 1988) was a Brazilian rubber tapper, union leader and environmental activist in the state of Acre. He organized rubber tappers to defend the forest against clearing for cattle ranching and was murdered in December 1988.

Chico Mendes was born on 15 December 1944 near Xapuri, Acre, into a family of rubber tappers (seringueiros).

He helped found the rural workers' union in Xapuri in 1977 and was among the founders of the Workers' Party in Acre in 1980.

He organized empates, non-violent standoffs in which tappers and their families stood in front of crews clearing forest.

In 1985 he helped found the National Council of Rubber Tappers, which promoted protected "extractive reserves" where residents could harvest forest products.

In 1987 he lobbied the Inter-American Development Bank in the United States over highway funding in the Amazon, and received a United Nations Environment Programme Global 500 award.
